| * [IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IATA_airport_code "IATA airport code"): _none_ * [ICAO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICAO_airport_code "ICAO airport code"): _none_ |
| Summary |
| Operator | [Aeronautical Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York") |
| Location | [The Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"), New York, US |
| Opened | 1908 |
| Closed | 1909 |
| [Coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system "Geographic coordinate system") | ![Image 1: Show location on an interactive map](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/WMA_button2b.png/20px-WMA_button2b.png)[40°51′0″N 73°51′20″W / 40.85000°N 73.85556°W](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&params=40_51_0_N_73_51_20_W_region:US-NY_type:airport) |
| Map |
| [![Image 2: Location of the aerodrome, green oval labeled "Morris Park Race Track"](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Map_of_the_south-east_Bronx_%281900%29.jpg/250px-Map_of_the_south-east_Bronx_%281900%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_the_south-east_Bronx_(1900).jpg "Location of the aerodrome, green oval labeled \"Morris Park Race Track\"") Location of the aerodrome, green oval labeled "Morris Park Race Track" |

The **Morris Park Aerodrome** was a short-lived [airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airfield "Airfield") in what is now the [Morris Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx "Morris Park, Bronx") section of [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"), New York, United States. The [aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerodrome "Aerodrome"), which was in operation from 1908 to 1909, was the first flying field in the nation, occupying the grounds of the former [Morris Park Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse "Morris Park Racecourse"). The [Aeronautical Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York"), after a split from the [Aero Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_Club_of_America "Aero Club of America"), leased the land in 1908 and used it as an aerodrome for two years until it was developed for residential use.

The Society used the grounds for building and testing aircraft, and for putting on public exhibitions including major events in November 1908, and June 1909. The former, captured in an oil painting by [Rudolph Dirks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Dirks "Rudolph Dirks") titled _The Fledglings_, included several glider flights by sixteen-year-old [Laurence Lesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_J._Lesh "Laurence J. Lesh"), culminating in a crash in which he was severely injured. The latter had flights by [Glenn Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Curtiss "Glenn Curtiss") in his _[Golden Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss\_No.\_1 "Curtiss No. 1")_ motorized biplane, including the first demonstration of a stable flight around a closed course using [ailerons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aileron "Aileron") for lateral control. The exhibitions also featured [balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balloon_(aeronautics) "Balloon (aeronautics)"), [kites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kite "Kite"), [helicopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicopter "Helicopter"), parachute jumps, and ground vehicles driven by propellers known as wind wagons.

Other projects worked on during the two years of operation included a biplane by Wilbur Kimball using eight propellors and a novel [rudder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder "Rudder") system for lateral control, and a biplane from Frederick Schneider with three adjustable-pitch [propellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller "Propeller"). Stanley Beach and Charles Willard constructed what is believed to be the first [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") flown in the United States. Joel T. Rice demonstrated a 100-foot (30 m) long dirigible using [vectored thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_vectoring "Thrust vectoring"), capable of carrying 15 passengers.

The aerodrome ceased operations at the end of 1909, when the land was given over to residential development. The Society moved its operations to a larger facility on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"), which would eventually become known as [Roosevelt Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Field_(airport) "Roosevelt Field (airport)").

> "What the Society needed in the way of ground was not very easy to find. Free, open space over which to fly was not alone sufficient. It was equally, if not, indeed, still more necessary, that the grounds should be close to the city. For it was the ambition of the Society to have its grounds so near at hand that the distance should place no obstacle in the way even of the poorest inventor who wanted to run out to the workshops and devote his spare hours to the material realization of his ideas."

Edward T. Tandy, An Epitome of the Work of The Aeronautic Society from July, 1908, to December, 1909

In 1905, the [Aero Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_Club_of_America "Aero Club of America"), patterned after the [Aero Club of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A%C3%A9ro-Club_de_France "Aéro-Club de France"), was formed as an offshoot of the [Automobile Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile_Club_of_America "Automobile Club of America"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-1) Three years later, in response to sentiment that the aero club should be more active, president [Cortlandt Field Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortlandt_F._Bishop "Cortlandt F. Bishop") appointed a Committee of Aviation chaired by [Albert Triaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_C._Triaca "Albert C. Triaca") to promote more work on aeroplanes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908b-2) The Committee, however, was unable to make any progress; Society chronicler Edward T. Tandy later wrote, "they found their efforts smothered by a cold, wet blanket of official objection. When they attempted to persevere, they were promptly stopped. The power that ruled that organization did not believe in aviation ... The doing of anything practical was not to be attempted."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 7–8

Unsatisfied with the progress being made by the committee, fifty members of the club split off on June 10, 1908, forming the [Aeronautical Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York"). Initial membership included Lee Burridge, Albert Triaca, [Willard Kimball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ravel_Kimball "Wilbur Ravel Kimball"), Roger Whitman, [William Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Joseph_Hammer "William Joseph Hammer"), [Leo Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Leo_Stevens "Albert Leo Stevens"), Daniel Brine, and [Stanley Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Yale_Beach "Stanley Yale Beach").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908b-2) Burridge (who would later be President of the Society[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-4)) spoke of plans to acquire an airfield: "this society is going to stand for something tangible, practical, and it proposes to secure experimental grounds as soon as possible where men who have been working on problems of aeronautics will be enabled to try out their machines".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908b-2)

That summer, the Society looked at several properties from [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") to [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island") and ultimately identified the grounds of the old [Morris Park Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse "Morris Park Racecourse") as the best location.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:8-5) The racecourse had closed in 1904, after which the 372-acre (151 ha) property was used for [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto_racing "Auto racing") and [motorcycle racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorcycle_racing "Motorcycle racing") for a few years. It was convenient to the recently opened [West Farms Square subway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Farms_Square%E2%80%93East_Tremont_Avenue_station "West Farms Square–East Tremont Avenue station") and a trolley stop, as well as a range of cafes and residences which could be had for inexpensive rents. Proximity to public transportation was considered essential, making the field accessible to all experimenters, not just the affluent.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 273–274

[![Image 3: Color picture postcard showing a three-story building in a wooded setting. Printed under the photo is "Woodmansten Inn, Pelham Parkway and Williamsbridge Road, Westchester, N.Y."](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Woodmansten_Inn_Postcard_%28front%29.webp/250px-Woodmansten_Inn_Postcard_%28front%29.webp.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woodmansten_Inn_Postcard_(front).webp)

The Woodmansten Inn

The location provided open spaces on a level elevation, several existing buildings which could be repurposed as workshops, and a larger building with a neatly trimmed lawn and flower beds to use as a clubhouse.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:9-7) The nearby Woodmansten Inn, built in 1902, had a restaurant and sleeping facilities.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:13-8) An advertisement in the 1908 exhibition program offered dinner with wine for $3.00 (equivalent to $74 in 2024)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:18-9): 4  and Tandy described it as "one of the best and most fashionable hotels of the city".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 9

Morris Park Aerodrome (occasionally called the Morris Park Volery[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909a-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:24-11)) was made available to members for the first time on the weekend of August 29 and 30, 1908.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 274  A lease was signed on or about August 31,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:8-5) running until December 31, 1909,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:3-12) although it was already known that the land was eventually destined for residential development.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 9  By the next week, fences adjacent to the track were being removed to provide a clear straight path of at least 0.62 miles (1.00 km), locations were being considered for constructing a machine shop, and plans were being made for an exhibition where "Freak machines will have a chance to show what they can do as well as the more orthodox types."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:3-12)

[![Image 4: Photograph of an ornate five-story building with multiple setbacks, balconies, and awnings.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/The_American_turf-_an_historical_account_of_racing_in_the_United_States_-_with_biographical_sketches_of_turf_celebrities._1898_%281898%29_%2817975359990%29.jpg/250px-The_American_turf-_an_historical_account_of_racing_in_the_United_States_-_with_biographical_sketches_of_turf_celebrities._1898_%281898%29_%2817975359990%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_American_turf-_an_historical_account_of_racing_in_the_United_States_-_with_biographical_sketches_of_turf_celebrities._1898_(1898)_(17975359990).jpg)

Morris Park Clubhouse in 1898

Morris Park was the first flying field in the United States[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-13) although by the end of 1909, _[All the World's Air-Ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janes\_All\_the\_World%27s\_Aircraft "Janes All the World's Aircraft")_ by [Fred Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_T._Jane "Fred T. Jane") listed it as one of eight such facilities in the country.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-14) The primary purpose of the field was the construction of aircraft, although it was also used for flight instruction, hosting Albert Tiiaca's International School of Aeronautics.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:9-7) Within the first 12 months of operation, 24 full-sized heavier-than-air airplanes were constructed on the field, plus an assortment of gliders, airships, and a large number of scale models. Almost 25% of the Society membership held aircraft patents or were directly involved in the construction of aircraft at the field.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 6

Lacking any hill high enough to launch a glider from, the Society built two facilities for assisting in glider launches. The first was a catapult. The second was a larger structure of wooden construction, which was erected without first obtaining a building permit. After a glider spent an entire day atop the structure waiting for winds favorable for launching, city officials declared that the structure was a residence, and since it lacked both plumbing and a fire escape, condemned it, compelling it to be torn down.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 14

Many of the aircraft built at Morris Park were failures, with aviation historians taking a pessimistic view of the members' skills. [Preston Bassett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Bassett "Preston Bassett") described the Aeronautic Society as "a group of enthusiastic young men in New York City, all with plans for building their own machines [whose] enthusiasm far outran their ability to perform".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:24-11) Paul Glenshaw, wrote "The group could boast of few successes. Descriptions of the members’ experiments included words like 'tree' and 'fence', coupled with 'plunged' and 'smashed'."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-15)

On October 18, the first exhibition of the Society was announced for November 3 to coincide with [election day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_United_States_presidential_election "1908 United States presidential election"). There were plans for two airplanes from the [Aerial Experiment Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_Experiment_Association "Aerial Experiment Association")_([June Bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA\_June\_Bug "AEA June Bug")_ and _[Silver Dart)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA\_Silver\_Dart "AEA Silver Dart")_ to compete, a five-mile [dirigible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship") race, [kites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kite "Kite"), and [gliders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glider_(aircraft) "Glider (aircraft)"); the kite contest was open to [public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_school "Primary school") students with no entry fee.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-16) There were also plans for one-, five-, and ten-mile [motorcycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorcycle "Motorcycle") races sponsored by the [Federation of American Motorcyclists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Motorcyclist_Association "American Motorcyclist Association")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 269  and for the [U.S. Weather Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") to demonstrate the use of kites and captive balloons to collect atmospheric data.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 277 [Lillian Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._Lilian_Todd "E. Lilian Todd"), the only female member of the Society,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-17) was expected to show a "large model airplane" of her own design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:18-9): 11

Admission to the exhibition was $0.50 (equivalent to $17.5 in 2024), with the [subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") ride from [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") taking 40 minutes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 269  An estimated 20,000 spectators showed up, far exceeding expectations. Although several hundred people had volunteered to act as marshals (equipped with badges and sticks), a large number of people swarmed past the gate with only about 3,500 people having paid their admission fee.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 279  Tandy wrote that in the years since the race track had been in use, the fences had deteriorated and that "The payment for admission proved a matter of almost quixotic courtesy."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 15

[![Image 5: A man hangs below a glider in flight. Many people (at least 100) are watching.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Lawrence_J._Lesh_in_Glider_Flight_at_Morris_Park.png/250px-Lawrence_J._Lesh_in_Glider_Flight_at_Morris_Park.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lawrence_J._Lesh_in_Glider_Flight_at_Morris_Park.png)

Lesh in the air at the 1908 exhibition

Sixteen-year-old glider pilot [Laurence J. Lesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_J._Lesh "Laurence J. Lesh") was the highlight of the exhibition. A protégé of aviation pioneer [Octave Chanute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Chanute "Octave Chanute"), Lesh was the first known aviator in Canada, having built and flown horse-drawn gliders as early as 1907 when he was fourteen years old. He became known for a record-setting 24 minute, 6.2-mile (10.0 km) flight towed by a motor boat on the [St. Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Lawrence_River "St. Lawrence River").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:0-18)

Lesh [broke his ankle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankle_fracture "Ankle fracture") when he crashed during his third flight of the day after reaching a maximum altitude of 70 feet (21 m) and travelling about 200 feet (61 m).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908a-19) One account attributed the cause of the crash to inexperience flying this model of glider which lacked the rudder used on his earlier designs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:10-20) Another account blamed the crowd which got in his way while attempting to land.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 17  In any case, the injuries sustained in the crash sent Lesh to the hospital and took a year of [rehabilitative therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_therapy "Physical therapy") to fully recover.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:0-18)

The glider had been launched by rope tow behind [a 1907 Thomas Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Motor_Company#New_York_to_Paris_Race "Thomas Motor Company") driven by [Montague Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montague_Roberts "Montague Roberts"), one of the drivers for the team who had won the [1908 New York to Paris Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_New_York_to_Paris_Race "1908 New York to Paris Race") in that car.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908a-19)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-21) Montague had also competed in a 1907 24-hour race held at Morris Park when it was used for automobile racing.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-22) Previous launch attempts on the day of the exhibition had used a tow horse; out of six tries, only two got off the ground, reaching an altitude of about 20 feet (6.1 m).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-23) Lesh had also planned to show a large [box kite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_kite "Box kite") that day.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-24)

[![Image 6: A man wearing a white shirt, tie, and cap sits on a three-wheeled vehicle. The wheels appear to be from a bicycle. In the rear is some machinery and a large propeller. The man is holding in one hand what appears to be a tiller for steering the front wheel, and in the other controls for the machinery.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Glenn_Curtiss_Seated_on_a_Wind_Wagon.png/250px-Glenn_Curtiss_Seated_on_a_Wind_Wagon.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Glenn_Curtiss_Seated_on_a_Wind_Wagon.png)

Glenn Curtiss on a wind wagon (date and location unknown)

The exhibition included a wind wagon contest, these being wheeled ground vehicles driven by propeller thrust.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-16)_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ described one of these as resembling "a huge tricycle with a propeller eight feet long in front and a gasoline motor behind".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-25) Inventors scheduled to show their wagons included astronomer [William Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Pickering "William Henry Pickering"), aviation pioneer [Glenn Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Curtiss "Glenn Curtiss"), W. A. Custard,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-16) and [Julian P. Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_P._Thomas "Julian P. Thomas").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:19-26) According to Curtiss, the purpose of the wind wagon was to test the power of motors and the efficiency of propellers[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-27) and it had no commercial value.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-28)

Thomas's machine was wrecked two days before the exhibition, when he crashed during a practice run while trying to avoid a motorcycle. About 40 motorcyclists were using the track to prepare for a race scheduled to be held on exhibition day; Thomas believed they had already cleared the track and entered the course, running at high speed. He sustained severe injuries which were initially thought to have been fatal, but after several minutes of [unconsciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconsciousness "Unconsciousness"), he opened his eyes, asked for a [cigarette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cigarette "Cigarette"), and refused to be taken to a hospital. Recuperating at home, Thomas asked that the machine be repaired so another driver could use it during the exhibition.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:19-26)

Two weeks after the 1908 exhibition, Lee Burridge spoke at the November 2 annual meeting of the Aero Club, reflecting on the schism which led to the founding of the Aeronautical Society. He complained of the "apathy of the Aero Club" when, after he had identified Morris Park as a potential site, they failed to act on the opportunity. [Augustus Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Post "Augustus Post"), secretary of the Aero Club, replied that doing so would have split the membership into two classes, to which he was opposed. Post added that the club was still seeking to "secure extensive grounds for motor ballooning and aeroplaning, with [hydrogen gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifting_gas#Hydrogen "Lifting gas") facilities, [machine shops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_shop "Machine shop"), and suitable buildings for storage, within easy distance of the city".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:23-29)

Members of the opposition group who had split off to form the new society acknowledged that while Morris Park was too small, it would serve a temporary function while they continued to search for a larger facility. A motion authorizing the Aero Club to work together with the Aeronautical Society to jointly search for a location was discussed, but failed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:23-29)

[![Image 7: A biplane in flight. A man is visible at the controls.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Curtiss_Aeroplane_in_Flight_1909.png/250px-Curtiss_Aeroplane_in_Flight_1909.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Curtiss_Aeroplane_in_Flight_1909.png)

The Golden Flyer at Morris Park, 1909

A second annual exhibition was held on June 26, 1909, with 2000 people in attendance[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:1-30) on a day with ideal flying weather[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) but with near-record high temperatures.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:14-32) The low attendance left the Society with a $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024) deficit.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:14-32)

The highlight of the event was a series of flights by Curtiss in a [biplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biplane "Biplane") named the _[Golden Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss\_No.\_1 "Curtiss No. 1")_ which the Society had purchased from Curtiss and his partner [Augustus Herring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Moore_Herring "Augustus Moore Herring") for $5,000.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:11-33) This set a number of records; the flights themselves were the first airplane flights ever taken over New York City,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-34) the purchase was the first to a civilian owner, and the [Herring-Curtiss Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss_Aeroplane_and_Motor_Company "Curtiss Aeroplane and Motor Company") was the first aeroplane manufacturing company in the country.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:11-33) The terms of the sale included training for two pilots (Charles Willard and Alexander Williams[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-35)), and an obligation for Curtiss to fly it the exhibition. The Curtiss design used [ailerons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aileron "Aileron") for [roll control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_flight_control_system "Aircraft flight control system") instead of the [wing warping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing_warping "Wing warping") system employed by the [Wright Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_brothers "Wright brothers"), making the airplane more stable and more maneuverable.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-36)

> "That the defendant, alleging to be formed for the purpose of promoting aerial flying, procured the Herring-Curtiss Company and one Glenn H. Curtiss, personally, both of Hammondsport, N.Y., to make the flying machines herin complained of and deliver them to the defendant, under whose auspices the said Glenn H. Curtiss is giving public exhibition flights with the said infringing flying machines within the jurisdiction of this court; that the defendant has purchased such machines from one or both of said parties, and has charged the public for admission to said exhibition flights, receiving large sums in gate, or ticket, money."

Quote from Wright Brothers patent suit

The flight of the Golden Flyer created legal controversy when two months later the Wright Brothers filed a [patent infringement suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") against the Aeronautic Society in the [United States Circuit Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_circuit_court "United States circuit court"), claiming infringement of their 1906 patent. The suit ([one of many](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_brothers_patent_war "Wright brothers patent war") the Wrights would eventually file against competitors) demanded that the Society be permanently [injuncted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injunction "Injunction") from further infringement, disclose how much money had been made from the exhibitions, and turn over for destruction all "machinery, flying machines, and parts thereof" which infringed the patents.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-37)

The first flight was a straight-line flight covering 300 yards (270 m), averaging 30 feet (9.1 m) in altitude. _[The Brooklyn Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn\_Eagle "Brooklyn Eagle")_ noted that "his adjustment of his controls to uneven wind currents was absolutely accurate".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) The remainder of the flights took place after twilight, having been delayed by puffy winds, with the event being forced to conclude as darkness fell. The rough ground at the field was a complicating factor, making landings difficult.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:5-38) One flight lasted 1 minute 45 2/5 seconds, completing either three-quarters or a full lap (sources differ) around the 1-mile (1.6 km) track at an altitude of 20 feet (6.1 m), flying between trees along the [backstretch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backstretch "Backstretch") and sometimes reaching as high as 60 feet (18 m). The aircraft was reported as "always under perfect control".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:1-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) This flight was the first time Curtiss had completed a flight around a circular course, although [Henri Farman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Farman "Henri Farman") and the Wright Brothers had both already accomplished this feat.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-39) Curtiss had hesitated before making the turn at the north end of the track, which had been criticized as being too confining.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:14-32)

[![Image 8: An aircraft in flight, just barely above the ground. It is banked at approximately 45 degrees.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/William_Martin_Glider_at_Morris_Park_1909.png/250px-William_Martin_Glider_at_Morris_Park_1909.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_Martin_Glider_at_Morris_Park_1909.png)

William Martin's glider at Morris Park

William H. Martin flew a glider towed by an automobile driven by his wife. He had only gone about 50 yards (46 m) when the tow rope broke and the glider crashed; he suffered minor injuries but the aircraft was severely damaged.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:1-30) The safety of the craft was demonstrated on September 21 when Martin's eight-year-old granddaughter, Blanche, made several solo flights, becoming the youngest person to make a flight in a heavier-than-air craft.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:4-40)

Martin's glider had originally been constructed on his farm in [Canton, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Ohio "Canton, Ohio"), equipped with sled runners for operation on snow. The V-shaped lower wings added stability as a result of the [dihedral effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dihedral_(aeronautics) "Dihedral (aeronautics)"). It first flew on January 12, 1909, launched from the top of a hill and towed by Martin's horse named Old Billy. The first flight covered 200 feet (61 m) reaching a maximum altitude of 25 feet (7.6 m). Over the next few days, over 100 flights were conducted, with Martin's wife, son, and pet dog all taking turns. Martin brought the glider to Morris Park in May 1909, where it continued to make demonstration flights, being pulled around the track at 30 miles per hour (48 km/h) behind an automobile with a 150 ft (46 m) tow rope, and reaching altitudes as high as 75 feet (23 m). By this time, the snow runners had been replaced with wheels.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:4-40)

The UK-based [Flight Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_International "Flight International") called the Martin glider demonstration the most notable event of the day, after Curtiss's flight. They took a negative view, however, of Martin's craft, calling it an "example of the foolhardiness of tests of this character" and writing that "there is little or nothing to be learned through being towed behind a car in this manner ... the conditions do not represent the problems of flight in the least". They described the flight as a "short and erratic aerial journey". They noted that the presence of the tow rope restricted operation the aircraft and negatively affected its stability.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-41)

### Additional exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Additional exhibits")]

Frederick Schneider demonstrated a motor-driven [catapult-assisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_catapult "Aircraft catapult") airplane of his own construction, named _The Brooklyn_. The craft failed to get off the ground due to a rusty launching rail and too little weight loaded into the catapult, only managing to slide along the grass for 100 feet (30 m). There were also [parachute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute "Parachute") jumps from [hot air balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_air_balloon "Hot air balloon"), with Paul Bloomfield jumping from 1,000 feet (300 m), and Mary Hunter from an altitude reported only as "far higher" than Bloomfield's.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) One of the less serious events was a "balloonatic race". This consisted of a person attempting to run while being supported by a lighter-than-air balloon with just enough buoyancy to support the person's weight.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:5-38)

[![Image 9: A scene of an aviation exhibition. Several winged craft are on the ground; some have propellers, some do not. A car appears to be pulling one of them. Dozens of people are milling around, some with bicycles. In the background, a boy flies a kite.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Detail_from_%22The_Fledglings%22.jpg/250px-Detail_from_%22The_Fledglings%22.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Detail_from_%22The_Fledglings%22.jpg)

Detail from _The Fledglings_

In attendance at the 1908 exhibition was painter [Rudolph Dirks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Dirks "Rudolph Dirks"), better known as the cartoonist who drew _[The Katzenjammer Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Katzenjammer\_Kids "The Katzenjammer Kids")_. Based on his experiences at the show, Dirks created an oil-on-linen painting titled _The Fledglings._[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2012-42) After the show, Dirks quickly returned to his [studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio "Studio") in Manhattan where he began work on the painting, working from some rough pencil sketches he had made at the show.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-43) Not having any prepared canvas on hand and wishing to begin work quickly so as not to let his memories of the event fade, Dirks repurposed a linen window shade to use as a canvas.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2012-42)

The painting is considered by aviation historian [Tom Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_D._Crouch "Tom D. Crouch") to be "the earliest serious artistic reaction to the dawn of the air age".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2012-42) It was donated by Dirks' son to the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") where, as of 2025, it is on display in the Early Flight exhibit.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-National_Air_and_Space_Museum_20112-44)

The base includes a semi-circular scale with a rotating pointer for measuring angles. The uprights have numbered scales going from 1 at the bottom to 8 at the top, with fractional marks between the numbers; the sliding cross-piece is positioned at position 7. Three strings run between the rotating pointer on the base to the cross-slide, describing a complex spiral shape.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Device_for_laying_out_a_propeller_by_R._W._Jamieson.png/250px-Device_for_laying_out_a_propeller_by_R._W._Jamieson.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Device_for_laying_out_a_propeller_by_R._W._Jamieson.png)

Device for laying out a propeller

The March 1909 issue of _[Aeronautics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics\_(magazine)#Early\_American\_magazine\_(1907%E2%80%931915) "Aeronautics (magazine)")_ included a paper by R. W. Jamieson describing a device used to lay out a [screw propeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller "Propeller") for an airplane, taking into account the diameter and [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_pitch "Blade pitch"). Jamieson described the layout process in a talk to the Society; the device itself was presented to the Society and installed at the Morris Park Aerodrome for use by the society's members.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-45)

A report in the April 1909 issue of _Aeronautics_ described new aircraft (referred to as "machines") that were being planned or under construction by at least twenty members of the Society and would be exhibited at Morris Park in the spring of that year. The report noted that [Anna Held](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Held "Anna Held") christened the first aeroplane constructed entirely at Morris Park.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-46) The magazine had previously observed that Americans often named their aircraft, contrary to the European habit of numbering them: "Flying machines have a something that is akin to a personality, and giving them names, even if it does not help us to realize their individuality, and perhaps it may, at least it helps in a curiously subtle way to popularize them."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909a-10)

[![Image 11: A biplane with multiple propellers sitting on the ground. Around it are approximately 40 men. A woman in fancy clothes is standing in front of the plane.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Kimball_aeroplane_being_christened_at_Morris_Park_Aerodrome%2C_1909.png/250px-Kimball_aeroplane_being_christened_at_Morris_Park_Aerodrome%2C_1909.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kimball_aeroplane_being_christened_at_Morris_Park_Aerodrome,_1909.png)

Anna Held christening the _N.Y. No. 1_ at Morris Park

[Wilbur R. Kimball's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ravel_Kimball "Wilbur Ravel Kimball") design was a 42-foot (13 m) wingspan biplane with eight four-bladed low-pitch propellers on ball-bearing mounts driven by a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four cylinder [two-stroke engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-stroke_engine "Two-stroke engine").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909b-47) Lateral control was achieved by a system similar to that used by J. Neale: four movable panels set vertically between the two wings (compared to two used by Neale).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-48) In addition to this airplane, Kimball was also working on another design for William H. Butler which would utilize a 100 horsepower (75 kW) engine.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909b-47) Kimball's airplane was christened on March 14 by Anna Held as the _N. Y. No. 1;_ the ceremony was believed to be the first time an aeroplane had ever been christened.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909a-10)

On December 4, 1909, a shed containing four of Kimball's aeroplanes was destroyed by fire. The value of the aeroplanes was estimated at $25,000 (equivalent to $620,000 in 2024).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-49)

### Frederick Schneider

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Frederick Schneider")]

In December 1908, a new airplane arrived at Morris Park: a biplane under construction by Frederick Schneider,[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-50) who had begun construction at his home in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), disassembled it there, delivered it to Morris Park on Christmas day, and had it reassembled by the 29th of December. The plane had a 30-foot (9.1 m) wingspan and with a pilot aboard weighed 630 pounds (290 kg) with a main wing loading of 1.7 pounds per square foot (8.3 kg/m 2). A 36 horsepower (27 kW) five-cylinder air-cooled engine drove three adjustable-pitch propellers.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909b-47)

### Stanley Beach and Charles Willard

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Stanley Beach and Charles Willard")]

[![Image 12: Head-on photograph of a monoplane. A man stands to the side of one wingtip.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Beach-Willard_Monoplane%2C_Charles_F._Willard_and_Stanley_Yale_Beach1.jpg/250px-Beach-Willard_Monoplane%2C_Charles_F._Willard_and_Stanley_Yale_Beach1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beach-Willard_Monoplane,_Charles_F._Willard_and_Stanley_Yale_Beach1.jpg)

Beach-Willard Monoplane

Stanley Beach and [Charles Willard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_F._Willard "Charles F. Willard") constructed a [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") at Morris Park patterned after those built by [Bleriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bl%C3%A9riot "Louis Blériot") and [Antoinette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoinette_(manufacturer) "Antoinette (manufacturer)").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:21-51) Completed on May 31, 1909, it was reported to be the first monoplane flown in the United States. Beach claimed it was faster than either the Wright or Curtiss airplanes, and just as stable. He intended to show it at the Hudson-Fulton Celebration, and fly it from New York to [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:20-52)

The aeroplane had a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four-cylinder [water cooled engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_cooling "Water cooling") and a [wing loading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing_loading "Wing loading") of 2-1/2 lbs per square foot.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-53) The engine ran at 1000 RPM, driving a nine foot propeller at 500 RPM via a [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_drive "Chain drive") via a 2:1 reduction [sprocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprocket "Sprocket").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:20-52) During early testing, the propeller turning at 300 RPM developed 325 pounds (147 kg) of [thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust "Thrust").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-54) A July 1909 report in _Aeronautics_ gives a wingspan of 38 ft (11.6 m) and a weight of 750 pounds (340 kg) including the pilot.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:21-51) A newspaper report in October, however, said it had a 41 ft (12.5 m) wingspan, weighed 1,100 pounds (500 kg) without the pilot, and was equipped with inflatable [pontoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Float_(nautical) "Float (nautical)") for water landings.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:20-52)

In July 1908, 24-year-old Henry W. Walden, a New York City dentist and aviation enthusiast, read about the Aeronautics Society. He joined in September of that year and began designing and building aeroplanes at Morris Park, despite a lack of training in aerodynamics. His first design, a [tandem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tandem "Tandem") biplane called the _Walden I_, was predicated on his belief that earlier designs lacked sufficient wing area. Ready for flight testing in early spring 1909, it used an automobile engine supplied to him by the Society. The 15 horsepower (11 kW) 500 lb (230 kg) engine proved unsuitable and he abandoned the design. His second effort, the _Walden II_, was completed in late May. This also failed to get off the ground. Walden attributed the failure to insufficient wing area and extended the wingsan by 2 feet (0.61 m) on each side, but it was destroyed in a windstorm before another attempt at flight could be undertaken.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:22-55)

Encouraged by watching Glenn Curtiss's flights at the June 1909 exhibition, Walden began work on the _Walden III,_ which he decided needed to be smaller and less complicated than his previous two. He designed a monoplane, purchasing a [three cylinder Anzani engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzani_3-cylinder_fan_engines "Anzani 3-cylinder fan engines") capable of producing 25–30 horsepower (19–22 kW). The wing was designed in a way which made it possible to add additional panels to increase the wing area if needed. To expedite construction, Walden hired two assistants to work on the plane, and another dentist to take over most of his practice. The plane was completed in late November, but by that time the Society's lease was running out and the plane was moved to [another field in Mineola, Long Island,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Field_(airport) "Roosevelt Field (airport)") where it was first test-flown on December 9.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:22-55)

American Eagle at Morris Park, 1909

In February 1908, aviator [Joel T. Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joel_T._Rice&action=edit&redlink=1 "Joel T. Rice (page does not exist)") (with financial backing from [John Andrew Riggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Andrew_Riggs "John Andrew Riggs")[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:6-56)) formed the [Hot Springs Airship Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Springs_Airship_Company "Hot Springs Airship Company") in [Hot Springs, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Springs,_Arkansas "Hot Springs, Arkansas") whereupon they started work on a [dirigible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship"), over 50-foot (15 m) long, named _The Arkansas Traveler._[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-57) In 1909, they moved the ship to New York, where they showed it at the [Hudson–Fulton Celebration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson%E2%80%93Fulton_Celebration "Hudson–Fulton Celebration"). They also began work at Morris Park on a larger ship, _The American Eagle,_ costing over $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024). At the time, this was the largest steel-framed airship in the country.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:6-56) The name was unpopular with New Yorkers, leading to the newspapers of the time referring to it as _The Arkansas Traveler_, the same name as the previous ship.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:7-58) Plans were being made for the [Seeing New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seeing_New_York "Seeing New York") company to use the ship for sightseeing tours over New York City.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-59)

_The American Eagle_ had a 100-foot (30 m) envelope holding 33,000 cubic feet (930 m 3) of gas with an 80-foot (24 m) compartment providing seating for 15 passengers.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:15-60) Instead of the usual rudder, she had a large propeller mounted so that in addition to providing propulsive thrust, it could [pivot left and right providing lateral control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_vectoring "Thrust vectoring"), Two smaller propellers could be pivoted up and down for vertical control, a system which Rice had patented in 1904. The ship included a system which captured and reused hydrogen gas that leaked from the envelope.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:16-61)

The ship was intended to be used for cross-country flights, with the initial trip scheduled from New York to [Washington DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."). Stops along the way were planned at 50–75-mile (80–121 km) intervals to show off the ship. Riggs said that the trip was intended "to demonstrate the practical uses of a properly equipped dirigible balloon for long-continued cross-country travel".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:16-61) Unfortunately, the flight never happened. Immediately after being launched, the horizontal planes accidentally hit the propellers, destroying them, making it impossible to control the ship. A gale-force storm two days later caused irreparable damage to the gas envelope.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:7-58)

[![Image 14: Vintage auction sale poster for Morris Park Race Track in the Bronx, New York City](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Auction_Sale_of_Morris_Park_Race_Track.pdf/page1-250px-Auction_Sale_of_Morris_Park_Race_Track.pdf.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Auction_Sale_of_Morris_Park_Race_Track.pdf)

Publicity booklet for Morris Park Race Track final auction.

Morris Park proved to be too small to serve the needs of the Aeronautical Society. After surveying the available locations near New York City, Glenn Curtiss recommended moving to the Hempstead Plains Aerodrome (later renamed [Roosevelt Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Field_(airport) "Roosevelt Field (airport)")), near [Mineola, Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineola,_New_York "Mineola, New York").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-62) On May 9 (another source says April 10[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:12-63)) 1910, a wind-blown fire destroyed the Morris Park property. The [Van Nest Hose Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Nest_Hose_Company "Van Nest Hose Company") responded, stopping trains on the [New Haven Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") for several hours because they needed to lay their hoses across the rails. Despite their efforts, the fire burned all afternoon consuming the race track and several nearby buildings.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:13-8) The property was later subdivided into building lots.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:12-63)

In the 1920s, there were efforts to create a new airport about 2 miles (3.2 km) to the northeast, in a marshy area near the [Hutchinson River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutchinson_River "Hutchinson River"), which was later the site of [Freedomland U.S.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedomland_U.S.A. "Freedomland U.S.A.") and, still later, of [Co-op City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-op_City,_Bronx "Co-op City, Bronx"). The Bronx Chamber of Commerce made one failed attempt in 1927. Another attempt in 1929 by [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright "Curtiss-Wright") failed when the [stock market crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929 "Wall Street crash of 1929").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-65)

7.title: Exploring the lost racecourses of New York City | Topics: Jerome Park, lost tracks, New York, Looking Back, Morris Park | Thoroughbred Racing Commentary
7.description: Article by Paul Roberts - Isabelle Taylor: Today, the city of New York lays claim to a single racecourse, Aqueduct, in operation since 1894. Little more than a century ago, however, the city boasted as many as seven courses. This article looks back to the golden age of racing in the Big Apple, with a review of some the lost racecourses of turn-of-the-century New York City.
7.content:
![Image 1: Illustrated scene showing an 1870s horse race and spectators, likely at the Saratoga race track](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/filer_public_thumbnails/drupal_files/brighton_beach_race_course_operated_in_brooklyn_from_1879_to_1908_image_via_the_library_of_congress.jpg__760x480_q85_crop_subsampling-2_upscale.jpg)

Brighton Beach Race Course operated in Brooklyn from 1879 to 1908. Image via the Library of Congress.

Today, the city of New York lays claim to a single racecourse, Aqueduct, in operation since 1894. Little more than a century ago, however, the city boasted as many as seven courses. This article looks back to the golden age of racing in the Big Apple, with a review of some the lost racecourses of turn-of-the-century New York City.

Thoroughbred racing in New York City dates back as far as 1665, when Gov. Richard Nicolls built a large, oval turf track on the open flatlands of Long Island known as Hempstead Plain. This was not only the first regular racecourse to be laid out in the city; it was, moreover, the first in the country. Christened Newmarket after the celebrated British forerunner, for more than a century all New York society, from gentry to farmers, flocked there. It gave rise to many imitators.

For many years, racing in the city was an ad hoc, localised pastime. The Civil War, however, turned the sport upside down. Whilst the bitter conflict caused racing’s collapse in nearly all Southern states, in the North it became a flourishing industry, regional even national in its scope. And at its centre was New York City.

Fundamental to this were two factors: the emergence of a new breed of tremendously rich capitalists and a heightened appetite for pleasure and entertainment in the aftermath of the ordeal of war. Into the racing milieu stepped millionaires such as August Belmont and D.D. Withers, who poured vast sums into building top-class stables and a spate of racecourses.

![Image 2: Jerome Park in present-day the Bronx, built in 1866 by millionaire businessman Leonard W. Jerome. Image via the Library of Congress.](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/drupal_files/Jerome%20Park%20in%20present-day%20the%20Bronx%2C%20built%20in%201866%20by%20millionaire%20businessman%20Leonard%20W.%20Jerome.%20Image%20via%20the%20Library%20of%20Congress.jpg)
Jerome Park in present-day the Bronx, built in 1866 by millionaire businessman Leonard W. Jerome. Image via the Library of Congress.

Jerome Park
-----------

Jerome Park was the most important of the new tracks. Laid out on 100 hectares (250 acres) in Fordham, just north of Manhattan, it opened its doors in 1866 as the brainchild of avid horseman Leonard W. Jerome. Up until that time, racing had something of an ignominious reputation in much of American society. Jerome, however, saw it as his quest to ennoble the sport from a “rowdies’ outing” into a “royal sport,” and to fulfil this he funded the most lavish racecourse ever seen on U.S. soil.

It consisted of a two-storey timber grandstand, measuring 140 metres (460 feet) long and capable of holding 8,000, and, on a large hill opposite, a spacious clubhouse. Comparable to a luxury hotel, it included a ballroom, dining room, and even an art gallery.

“Driving and sleighing parties, trap shooting, skating and polo playing rendered the place a favourite tryst. Sleeping accommodations were plenty and it became quite the thing for an owner to take a party of friends to dinner, stop overnight and be up betimes to see the morning gallops.” noted a 1901 article in _Outing_ magazine.

According to _Outing_, the clubhouse “soon became the great society rendezvous.”

Whilst racing in contemporary Britain and France, for instance, was an unmissable entry in the social season, Jerome Park vaulted this to a different level in New York. “Jerome Park on a raceday became a Mecca of fashion,” wrote Walter Vosburgh. Its principal _raison d’être_ was not the cultivation of the sport, but the cultivation of society and, in turn, commerce. Its admission policies were exclusive; especially compared to most British courses where infield admittance was free, entrance tickets were expensive, since, together with pool privileges and concessions, they provided the bulk of the revenue that enabled the racecourse to sustain itself without large audiences. This rationale gave rise to the design approach of set-piece buildings and also the genesis of the clubhouse building type.

From the day of its opening, when an estimated 30,000 clamoured through its gates, Jerome Park was a success. In 1890, though, it was dealt a death blow when the city requisitioned the land to build a reservoir. Nonetheless, as _The New York Times_ commented upon its inauguration in 1866, “as an event in the progress of the sport, it open[ed] an era.” It had helped to vault Thoroughbred racing to a new prominence amongst the metropolis’s pleasure seekers, so that by the last decade of the century, there were six courses running in and around New York City.

Such proximity inevitably bred competition, and the life expectancy of each course was not long. Securing the attention and patronage of the race-going public was imperative. Elegant settings and commodious buildings were one means of so doing, as consummately demonstrated at Morris Park Racecourse.

![Image 3: The palatial clubhouse of Morris Park, opened 1889. Image via Turnberry Consulting.](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/drupal_files/The%20palatial%20clubhouse%20of%20Morris%20Park%2C%20opened%201889.%20Image%20via%20Turnberry%20Consulting.jpg)
The palatial clubhouse of Morris Park, opened 1889. Image via Turnberry Consulting.

Morris Park
-----------

Morris Park opened its doors on Aug. 20, 1889, built as a result of the planned closure of Jerome Park. It was perhaps the first example in America of a consummately planned, architect-designed racecourse whose architecture and landscape was deliberately intended as a vantage over its competitors.

Its owner, John A. Morris, was a New Jersey businessman known widely as the “Lottery King” for his majority share in the Louisiana State Lottery. His chief ambition, it was said, was to own the finest Thoroughbred course in the world, and in 1888, he purchased 125 hectares (309 acres) in an area now part of the Bronx to make this a reality.

The track comprised a long grandstand, connected on its south elevation via an enclosed walkway to a spacious clubhouse. Five storeys tall, the clubhouse was a red brick and stone building.

“At Morris Park the race-goer has every chance to the greatest enjoyment from the ‘sport of kings,’ for all possible accommodations for his comfort are provided,” enthused _Outing_ in 1892. “The club-house is not the mere cottage which generally answers the purpose, but a magnificent building, fitted throughout not with consummate luxury and good only money, but taste, every feature, from the ball-room down, being elaborated regardless of expense.”

[![Image 4: Poster for the NZ National Yearling Sales Series 1927-2026, with an illustration of a racehorse being led by a person on a rural farm](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/filer_public/e4/6c/e46cbbb8-0ef9-4f88-a65f-2052c4b6f14b/nzb_100_years_750x150.jpg) ![Image 5: NZ National 1927-2026 Yearling 100 Years Sales Series features a black and white image of men in hats looking at a horse in an enclosure](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/filer_public/71/52/7152f269-cb5c-49d5-bbd3-af13edda9300/nzb_100_years_600x400.jpg)](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/adverts/redirect/?id=0454e6e6-65fe-47f8-b324-ba85d0575d68)

The grandstand was longer and lower than the clubhouse, seating 8,000 on a single tier accessed from the lawn apron via nine broad stairways. It was a wooden structure built on a base of supporting stone, iron, and brick arches. It was a simpler, less stately edifice than the clubhouse, but still incited popular praise: “On opening day the public will find seats on a stand which surpasses those of Flemington, Ascot, Longchamps, or Buenos Ayres [sic], which have had, until this palatial structure came into being, the best in the world,” rhapsodised _The New York Times_.

The opulence and scale of Morris Park was demonstrative of the nature of American racecourses. Run by financiers and businessmen such as Jerome and Morris, the tracks were commercial enterprises that needed to turn a profit. They were built to be fashionable venues, whose clubhouses bustled with New York society.

Morris Park illustrated, though, that even the most luxurious tracks could become victims of that fashion. In 1904, following a decline in attendance caused at least in part by competition from other city racecourses, Morris Park closed its doors for the last time.

![Image 6: 1894 map showing the three Brooklyn tracks and the railways serving them. Image via Art Huneke.](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/drupal_files/Option%201_%201894%20map%20showing%20the%20three%20Brooklyn%20tracks%20and%20the%20railways%20serving%20them.%20Image%20via%20Art%20Huneke.jpg)
1894 map showing the three Brooklyn tracks and the railways serving them. Image via Art Huneke.

The Brooklyn Circuit
--------------------

By the time of Morris Park’s closure, the cynosure of racing in New York City had transferred to Brooklyn. The first of Brooklyn’s three tracks, Brighton Beach, opened in 1879. From the outset, it was conceived to attract the crowds and reap a profit. It was built by William A. Engeman, an entrepreneur who bought several hundred acres of oceanfront property in Coney Island, which he named after the famous British seaside town and set about transforming it into a resort for New York crowds.

Not content with building only a pier, hotel, and bathing pavilion, Engeman decided that Brighton Beach also needed its own racecourse. In a little more than a month, with some 500 labourers working day and night, Engeman’s track opened on June 28, 1879. Two grandstands – capable of accommodating 13,000 racegoers – overlooked a mile-long track.

![Image 7: Sheepshead Bay Race Track, operated by the Coney Island Jockey Club, opened its doors in 1880. Image via Library of Congress.](https://www.thoroughbredracing.com/media/drupal_files/Sheepshead%20Bay%20Race%20Track%2C%20operated%20by%20the%20Coney%20Island%20Jockey%20Club%2C%20opened%20its%20doors%20in%201880.%20Image%20via%20Library%20of%20Congress.jpg)
Sheepshead Bay Race Track, operated by the Coney Island Jockey Club, opened its doors in 1880. Image via Library of Congress.

As Brighton Beach was taking shape, Leonard Jerome and other members of the American Jockey Club also recognised an opportunity in Coney Island. In 1879, some of the most powerful men in U.S. turf – including Jerome, August Belmont Jr, James R. Keene, A. Wright Stanford, and William R. Travers – banded to form the Coney Island Jockey Club and quickly announced the building of a new track in Sheepshead Bay. It opened in June 1880.

As well as stands to hold 40,000, Sheepshead Bay Race Track boasted a steeplechase track, training track, saddling paddock, judges’ stand, and betting ring. In 1886, it also included a turf course.

Thanks to the expertise, influence, and deep pockets of its founders, Sheepshead Bay was immediately successful. It drew the finest horses and horsemen, as well as high society and high bettors, and hosted two of the greatest fixtures of the era, the Suburban Handicap and the Futurity.

New York’s appetite for racing was still not sated, though. In 1886, brothers Phil and Mike Dwyer formed the Brooklyn Jockey Club, and began racing at the old Prospect Park trotting grounds in Gravesend. The Dwyers were businessmen, but they were also enthusiastic turfites. Their stable ranked amongst the best in the country, producing a Kentucky Derby winner and five Belmont Stakes victors.

The Gravesend Race Track opened on Aug. 26, 1886. Its physical environment did not compete with the glamour of many of its peers, but its running of the Preakness and Brooklyn Handicap drew audiences of tens of thousands.

Together, Gravesend, Sheepshead, and Brighton Beach became the biggest employer in Brooklyn. The tracks pioneered Monday-Saturday racing, beginning in spring at Gravesend and running until autumn, with racing alternating between the three venues. Racegoers were carried there by one of the most expansive railway systems in the country, running trains every 15 minutes.

Yet their popularity could not withstand the state prohibition of gambling in New York, decreed in 1910. The Agnew-Hart legislation closed every racecourse in the state. The Thoroughbred industry there collapsed, as trainers and horses were shipped overseas. Despite a reversal of the ban in 1913, Brighton Beach, Gravesend, and Sheepshead Bay never re-opened. The days of racing in Brooklyn were over, and the cynosure of New York turf settled permanently in Queens at the newer courses of Aqueduct and Jamaica, and in Long Island beyond the city boundaries at Belmont Park.

---

Authored by Paul Roberts and Isabelle Taylor. Condensed from[Racecourse Architecture](http://www.amazon.com/Racecourse-Architecture-Paul-Roberts/dp/092649483X), by Paul Roberts and Isabelle Taylor.

· N. Di Brino,_[The History Of The Morris Park Racecourse and Morris Family](http://www.amazon.com/History-Morris-Park-Racecourse-Family/dp/B0089DECGS)_, New York: Nicholas di Brino, 1977

· J. Dizikes, _[Yankee Doodle Dandy: The Life and Times of Tod Sloan](http://yalepress.yale.edu/book.asp?isbn=9780300083347)_, New Haven: Yale University Press, 2000

· _The New York Times_, 12 May 1889

Morris Park Racecourse
======================

The Westchester Racing Association, under the leadership of majority shareholder, John Albert Morris, acquired 152 acres in 1888 on the outskirts of what was then referred to as Bear Swamp, and was later annexed into the Bronx, New York City. Morris Park was constructed to fill the anticipated void after the projected closing of nearby Jerome Park Racetrack. Jerome Park’s developer, Leonard W. Jerome, served as Morris Park’s president.

When the racecourse opened in August of 1889, it was touted as the “finest rack track in the world,”1 with a grandstand capacity of 15,000, a 1½ -mile track, its Eclipse track that ran diagonally across the main track on a ¾-mile straightaway, and 1,000-stall stables. Morris Park was accessible by horse and buggy and a new railroad line spur that brought fans to the track from the New York City boroughs and beyond.

Hall of Famer Isaac Murphy rode at Morris Park’s opening day in 1889, and the racecourse hosted both the Belmont Stakes and the Preakness in June of 1890. The Preakness was later restarted at Gravesend Race Track on Coney Island, but the Belmont Stakes continued to be held at Morris Park until it moved to the newly constructed Belmont Park on Long Island in 1905. In its brief 15-year history, Morris Park was also home to the Ladies Handicap, the Metropolitan Handicap, the Matron Stakes, and the Champagne Stakes. Additionally, Aqueduct’s Toboggan Handicap traces its roots to a six-furlong race on Morris Park’s Eclipse track, referred to as the “Toboggan Slide.”

Due to declining attendance and club memberships and the imminent opening of Belmont Park, the Westchester Racing Association elected to close Morris Park at the turn of the 20 th century.It held its final day of races on October 15, 1904.
