From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Horse racing course in the Bronx, New York

[![Image 13: Morris Park Race Track Van Nest with an old building and a racing track](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/The_Great_north_side%2C_or%2C_Borough_of_the_Bronx%2C_New_York_%281897%29_%2814578537047%29.jpg/250px-The_Great_north_side%2C_or%2C_Borough_of_the_Bronx%2C_New_York_%281897%29_%2814578537047%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Great_north_side,_or,_Borough_of_the_Bronx,_New_York_(1897)_(14578537047).jpg)

1897

**Morris Park Racecourse** was an American [thoroughbred horse racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoroughbred_horse_race "Thoroughbred horse race") facility from 1889 to 1904. It was located in a part of [Westchester County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County,_New_York "Westchester County, New York") that was annexed into [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx") in 1895 and later developed as the neighborhood of [Morris Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx "Morris Park, Bronx"). The racecourse was the site of the [Belmont Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Stakes "Belmont Stakes") from 1890 through 1904 as well as the [Preakness Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preakness_Stakes "Preakness Stakes") in 1890.

History
-------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Racecourse&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Morris Park Racecourse was conceived and built by majority shareholder [John Albert Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Albert_Morris "John Albert Morris") as a result of the planned closure of the nearby [Jerome Park Racetrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Park_Racetrack "Jerome Park Racetrack"), where racing ended in 1894 to make way for the [Jerome Park Reservoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Park_Reservoir "Jerome Park Reservoir"). Principal owner John Morris had extensive business interests in [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana") and the prominent New York businessman and horseracing enthusiast [Leonard W. Jerome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_W._Jerome "Leonard W. Jerome") served as the racecourse's president. [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American")[Racing Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Racing_and_Hall_of_Fame "National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame") jockey [Isaac Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Burns_Murphy "Isaac Burns Murphy") rode on opening day at the new facility—August 20, 1889—and Morris Park was described as "the finest race track in the world."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-2) Accessible by horse and buggy, the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") added a short spur from its main line near the [Van Nest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Nest,_Bronx "Van Nest, Bronx") station that brought racing fans directly to the new race track from the greater [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") area.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-nyt1889-05-12-3)

The track held the [USA Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Cross_Country_Championships "USA Cross Country Championships") from 1890 to 1892 and 1897 to 1898.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-4)

On June 10, 1890, Morris Park Racecourse hosted both the Preakness and Belmont Stakes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-5) While the Preakness Stakes was canceled for three years then restarted in 1894 at [Gravesend Race Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravesend_Race_Track "Gravesend Race Track") on [Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island "Coney Island"), the Belmont Stakes was held at Morris Park until it moved to [Belmont Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Park "Belmont Park") on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island") in 1905. During this same period of 1890 through 1904, the [Champagne Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_Stakes_(United_States) "Champagne Stakes (United States)") and the [Ladies Handicap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies_Handicap "Ladies Handicap") were also raced here. The [Metropolitan Handicap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Handicap "Metropolitan Handicap") was inaugurated here in 1891 as was the [Matron Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matron_Stakes_(United_States) "Matron Stakes (United States)") the following year.

A few days before he died in May 1895, John Morris leased the racecourse, with an option to purchase, to the Westchester Racing Association. Although the 1½ mile racecourse was modified to a one-mile circuit to allow for better spectator viewing, a lack of patronage by [high society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_class "Upper class") members meant the clubhouse was usually empty. By 1902, the decline in attendance resulted in the decision to close Morris Park Racecourse.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-6) The final day of races was held on October 15, 1904, and racing shifted to the new Belmont Park the following year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-7)

[![Image 14: Monochrome photograph captures the scene at a racetrack, with spectators lining the track and in the stands, and a row of cars parked nearby](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Auto_racing_at_Morris_Park_1907.jpg/250px-Auto_racing_at_Morris_Park_1907.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Auto_racing_at_Morris_Park_1907.jpg)

Auto racing at Morris Park, 1907

After its closure, the Morris Park Racecourse was used for [automobile racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile_racing "Automobile racing") but a few years later the Morris heirs sold the property to real estate developers. The new owners ran into financial problems which resulted in the track being taken over by the City of New York in 1907. The city then leased it for two years to the [Aeronautic Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York") who [used it as an aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome "Morris Park Aerodrome") and hosted the first public [air show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_show "Air show") on the grounds. In June 1909, [Glenn H. Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_H._Curtiss "Glenn H. Curtiss") put on a flying exhibition at Morris Park.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-8)

On April 10, 1910 a fire ravaged much of the stables and nearby facilities.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-9) Three years later the property was auctioned off to developers who would subdivide the land into building lots. As late as 1921 the clubhouse was still intact when it was sold as part of a 14-lot package to a company who converted it for use as a factory to manufacture [ornamental iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornamental_iron "Ornamental iron").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-10)

Physical attributes
-------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Racecourse&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Physical attributes")]

[![Image 15: Morris Park is shown in the center, with the long axis of the track oval oriented northwest-southeast. It is connected by Pelham Parkway to the large Pelham Bay Park to the northeast. The New York, New Haven, and Hartford rail line runs very close to the southeast edge of the property. To the west if Old Boston Road and beyond that Bronx Park](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Bronx_transit_and_landmarks_in_1896_%28NY_Times%29_-_re-tinted.png/250px-Bronx_transit_and_landmarks_in_1896_%28NY_Times%29_-_re-tinted.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronx_transit_and_landmarks_in_1896_(NY_Times)_-_re-tinted.png)

1896 _New York Times_ map showing the location of Morris Park and other major landmarks in the Bronx

Morris Park Racecourse was situated in the area bounded on the south by Sackett Avenue and by what is today the [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak")[Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") railroad right-of-way, on the east by Williamsbridge Road, on the west by what is now Bronxdale Road, and on the north by [Pelham Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelham_Parkway_(road) "Pelham Parkway (road)"). The grandstand stood at the intersection of Bogart and Fowler Avenues and the clubhouse was near the intersection of Fowler and Van Nest Avenues.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-12)

The racetrack covered 360 acres (1.5 km 2) and had a grandstand 650 feet (200 m) long that could accommodate up to 15,000 attendees. The main track had circumference of 1+1⁄2 mi (2.4 km), with a stretch that was 2,250 feet (690 m) long and widened from 80 feet (24 m) at the top of the homestretch to 240 feet (73 m) at the finish line. The north end of the track was located on a hill so horses had to run uphill on the backstretch and downhill on the homestretch. A [chute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chute_(racecourse) "Chute (racecourse)") on the main track permitted races of 1+1⁄8 mi (1.8 km) to be run with one turn. Another track called the Eclipse course ran diagonally across the main track on a straightaway of 3⁄4 mi (1.2 km), joining the main track at its finish line. It was named after Eclipse, a horse owned by Francis Morris. A six furlongs race on the Eclipse course was nicknamed the "Toboggan Slide" and continues to be run today at [Aqueduct Racetrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueduct_Racetrack "Aqueduct Racetrack") as the [Toboggan Handicap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toboggan_Handicap "Toboggan Handicap"). The stables at Morris Park Racecourse held a total of 1,000 stalls, more than any two of the other American racetracks combined.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-nyt1889-05-12-3)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse#cite_note-14)

Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history
===========================================================

By Ben Kochman Posted on [June 10, 2014](https://www.bxtimes.com/archivist-hopes-morris-park-will-honor-its-aviation-history/)

![Image 9: Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history](https://www.bxtimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/21-airport-2014-05-22-bx01_z.jpg?quality=51&w=500)

Photo by Ben Kochman||

The old Morris park racetrack is famous – but how about some love for the Morris Park Aerodrome?

A local historian hopes his efforts to recognize his hometown’s unique aviation past will get off the ground.

Morris Park is well known for its namesake racetrack, which hosted the Belmont Stakes from the mid-19th century until 1904. But an archivist at Fordham Prep has tracked down evidence that the east Bronx neighborhood was once also home to some of the world’s first glimpses of flying machines.

**First helicopter flight**

“There’s very little of Morris Park history that we celebrate and put out on public display, “ said Louis DiGiorno, who came across his nabe’s aviation past while researching Fordham Prep alumni, many of whom were pilots. “With something this important, we should think about marking it.”

In 1908, the New York Aeronautical Society rented out the former Morris Park racetrack and invited some of the world’s aviation inventors – including the creator of the helicopter – to try out their flying machines at the site.

“Wilbur H. Kimbull’s heliocopter, upon which he has been working for several years, is being assembled at Morris Park and by the end of the week he expects to be ready to try the ascensional power of the machine,” read a story in the September 7, 1908 New York Times.

The airplanes that made it into the air did not go far. The show’s organizers removed the fences around the old racetrack to create an “unobstructed straightway for a flight of at least one kilometer,” according to the Times.

Trust us: Here’s a photo of The Aeronautic Society of New York testing its flying machines in Morris Park in 1908.

Some of the machines were able to take off — others just looked very impressive.

“The airplane that won design for best airplane couldn’t even fly,” said borough historian Lloyd Ultan.

**Proposed plaque**

The racetrack burned down a few years later, said Ultan, before the land was auctioned off in 1913 to residential real estate developers.

DiGiorno has proposed a plaque or flag in recognition of the area’s aviation history to Community Board 11.

He’s even got a neighborhood tagline ready:

“Morris park: looking up since 1908.”

The Katzenjammer Kids Take to the Air
=====================================

It took a cartoonist to paint the first serious depiction of aircraft flight.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Tom Crouch](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/author/tom-crouch/)

![Image 4: No fan of aviation, Rudolph Dirks was persuaded by a friend to attend the air meet.](https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/T9w5Hh9MsXTRp1YIT9SV78jWdWc=/631x300/filters:no_upscale()/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer/In_the_Museum_Katzenjammer_1_FLASH.jpg)

 No fan of aviation, Rudolph Dirks was persuaded by a friend to attend the air meet. The “bizarre carnival atmosphere” delighted the artist, who rushed home to paint “The Fledglings,” considered the first serious artistic attempt to depict aircraft flight. NASM

On November 3, 1908, Rudolph Dirks, a 31-year-old newspaper artist, cartoonist, and aspiring painter, joined 20,000 fellow New Yorkers streaming out of their urban neighborhoods and heading to Morris Park in the Bronx. Notices distributed around the city over the past week had announced that the well-known horse and automobile racetrack was now an “aerodrome,” the site of an exhibition and tournament sponsored by the Aeronautic Society of New York.

Powered By

![Image 5: A 0x0 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?)![Image 6: A 1x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?)![Image 7: A 0x0 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?)![Image 8: A 0x0 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?)

The program for the event sounded promising. A five-cent, 40-minute subway ride from Manhattan plus a 50-cent entrance fee would give spectators a look at the wonders of the dawning aerial age. Advertised were “distance races for gliders” and “wind wagon pursuit races,” men shot from catapults, and competitions between balloon and parachute descents.

Not one of the powered machines on display would leave the ground that day, or any other, and the only glider pilot to take to the sky during the meet, 16-year-old Laurence Lesh, ended up with a broken ankle. Still, the crowd was treated to the sight of balloons and kites in the air, and was able to examine the winged craft up close.

Rudy Dirks, more excited by the crowd than by the flying machines, rushed back to his 14th Street studio eager to capture the scene while it was fresh in his mind. With no prepared canvas available, he tore down a large linen window shade, stretched it, and began a large oil painting, which he would title “The Fledglings.” While he had serious aspirations as an artist, he was already famous as the creator of the pioneering comic strip “The Katzenjammer Kids,” and that background shows. The painting he started that day has the feel of a single frame of a comic strip, with the lively crowd surging across the scene, milling around the aircraft, and even climbing into the trees.

More than any photograph of the period, Dirks’ painting captures the energy of a crowd gathered for their first glimpse of winged craft, which were just beginning to carry humans into the air. Across the painting stretches a fantastic assortment of flying machines. Most are the work of dreamers whose imaginations were not yet bound by technological reality. Still, some of the craft were airworthy. The biplane on the right of the canvas is obviously one of the large gliders constructed by the brothers Adolph and Charles Wittemann, who had begun advertising themselves as aeronautical engineers, based on Staten Island, as early as 1906.

The biplane glider with the wingtips drawn together, second from the left, is almost certainly Laurence Lesh’s aircraft. For those in attendance, the red automobile poised to tow the glider aloft would have been one of the big draws. It is the Thomas Flyer, just back from its victory in a New York-to-Paris race in which it had traveled west across North America, Asia, and Europe.

By squinting and using some imagination, we might guess that the high-wing craft, second from the right, with one group of men pulling it and a fellow at the rear pushing, is a glider that Aeronautic Society member Louis Adams purchased from Gustave Albin Whitehead, a controversial figure from Bridgeport, Connecticut, who claimed to have flown a powered aircraft two years before the Wrights. If he had, he must have forgotten the secret of his accomplishment, for there is no indication that Whitehead, who lived to see Lindbergh fly the Atlantic, ever left the ground again.

The strange craft with the drooping biplane wings (far left) may well be a large model produced by Arthur Mitchell. Perhaps Dirks’ memory of the wing configuration was incorrect, or perhaps the craft had suffered a serious accident, as the figure in the tree and the individuals clustered at the rear of the machine suggest.

Over the next few years, Henri Rousseau, Pablo Picasso, Robert Delaunay, and a handful of other European artists would begin to portray the impact winged flight had on society and culture. But Rudy Dirks led the way. “The Fledglings” pre-dates the work of those far better known painters, and stands as the earliest serious artistic reaction to the dawn of the air age. Thanks to the generosity of John Dirks, the painter’s son, “The Fledglings” is now in the collection of the National Air and Space Museum, and will soon be displayed in the Museum’s Early Flight gallery.

Morris Park Racecourse tunnel exposed
=====================================

by Bill Twomey Posted on [May 5, 2010](https://www.bxtimes.com/morris-park-racecourse-tunnel-exposed/)

Tom Vasti is very knowledgeable about the history of Morris Park, even the [minutiae.It](http://minutiae.it/) was no surprise therefore that when he noticed a large street opening on Bronxdale Avenue on March 4 that he stopped to examine it.There is an area behind Con Edison’s Building #21 where it is quite evident that an opening was closed off with a wall just behind the building just north of the Bronxdale Avenue entrance to the Con Edison Yard.A check of old maps shows that the walled off area led to a tunnel which served as the grand entrance to the Morris Park Race Course used by some of the most prized race horses of the day owned by such luminaries as August Belmont, John A. Morris, the Vanderbilts, et al.

A New Haven Railroad spur deposited the race horses and fans next to this tunnel.They entered on the west side of Bear Swamp Road, now Bronxdale Avenue, which led to the 20,000-seat grandstand and the clubhouse on the east side. The race course opened officially on August 20, 1889 and the last race there was held in 1904 after which the races moved to Belmont Park.The old racetrack took on a variety of uses including bicycle and auto racing along with pioneer aviation activities.The 307-acre track was finally auctioned off in 1913 after having changed hands a couple of times during which time the City of New York began laying out a street grid.

The street opening of early March unearthed the tunnel which was opened over a century ago and personally approved by John A. Morris.Vasti knew what he was looking at and immediately called Nick DiBrino, the author of “The History of the Morris Park Racecourse” and the recognized authority on the subject.DiBrino responded at once and began taking pictures and interviewing the owners of the construction company doing the excavation.The open trench was 14’ deep and held a considerable amount of dirt and debris.He also noted that the tunnel was lined with huge brown sandstone blocks.A couple of blocks had been removed and weighted approximately three tons each.These were placed on the side of the road and Nick dutifully photographed them.

The contractors were very responsive and kept DiBrino up to date on any new discoveries.When they found a buried stairway on March 18 at the east side of the street, they called Nick asking him to come over and examine it in the morning.They had exposed six steps of a 20’ wide stairway while Nick watched.The sandstone blocks were approximately 5’ x 4’ and weighed about three tons each.The roadway of Bronxdale Avenue had been reconstructed circa 1912-13 at which time the tunnel was filled.The only disturbance to the tunnel was in 1928 when holes were bored through it for various conduits to the Borden’s milk plant on the east side of the avenue.A school is now under construction at the old Borden’s site.

For years the question of whether or not the old tunnel was backfilled has finally been answered.Another old historical poser has been answered dispelling all rumors thanks to the vigilance and diligence of Tom Vasti and Nick DiBrino along with that of a very helpful and cooperative contractor.

14.title: Aeronautic Society
14.content:
**The Aeronautic Society of New York was the first aeronautical society in the world

 to possess a machine that would fly. It was the first in the world to give a public demon-

 stration of successful human flight, showing that man had at last devised an apparatus

 enabling him to make a turn in the air as easily as a bird, as surely, and as safely.

It was the first club in the world to send a flying machine out into the country,

 that the men, women, and children, in the villages and on the farms, might see what this

 wonderful thing was like, and that interest might be created thereby.

It was not only ths first, but still the only aeronautical organization in the world

 that has produced such activity among its members that nearly one-fourth of its entire

 membership are patentees or actual builders of machines.

Many of the members have constructed their machines at private workplaces. But at

 the wrokshops of the Society, at Morris Park, no fewer than 24 full-sized, heavier-than-air

 machines have been built since the shops were opened twelve months ago. The workshops

 have also turned out several gliders and many models. There has, likewise, been built there

 the latgest successful airship yet made in the United States. Hardly a week has passed

 since the early part of the year without some machine or another being tried out.

As every man was carrying out his own ideas, threshing out some new principle or

 device, it was hardly to be expected that all the machines would fly. In many cases unfor-

 tunate accidents caused delay just as success appeared to be within grasp. Some of the 

 machines, too, are not yet completed, or are held up by the delays of the manufacturers of

 their motors.

Withal, the success attained was at once remarkable and gratifying. One year earlier

 it would have been incredible. Three macines built at Morris Park showed excellent

 performances in the air from their very first trials, and before their constructors had

 even themselves fully learned the art of navigating them.

One was so successful it carried not only one passenger in addition to the operator,

 but even two passengers; and this machine was notable as being the first ever made to be

 driven not by a special aeronautical motor, but by an ordinary stock automobile motor.

Another machine built at the Park although it did not fly, and its inventor, without

 waiting to correct its defects, cast it aside for a better model, was awarded a prize of $500

 for excellence of contstruction; and that was the first money prize ever won in America by

 a flying machine.

Other machines of members, but not built at Morris Park, won success by getting

 into the air, and have made their mark in various parts of the country.

Other members have devoted themselves to details. Some have, as the result, evolved

 aerial propellers that are of superior design. Others have worked on engines. Others have

 invented devices of great utility as building aids. Other have spread knowledge by building

 and exhibiting models and by giving lectures.

By its contests for models the Society has led to the evolution of much appartaus and

 many new ideas, some of which show the utmost promise, and will certainly be heard of

 before the new year is through. Among them is an aeroplane of entirely new design

 which has properties of stability and slowness of flight speed such as have hitherto been

 quite unattainable.

By its example the Society has led to the formation of practical classes of instruction

 in New York City, and the formation of several societies and clubs in different parts of the

 country. No place was visited by the Society's machine but, if a club or society were

 not already in existence there, one was formed as the immediate result of the visit of

 the machine and the interest it aroused.

This is a summary of results of which any young society may justifiable be proud as a 

 statement of the outcome of its eneregies in its first eighteen months of existence. But it by

 no means tells all. It says nothing of the difficulties overcome. It discloses nothing of the

 romances, ay, end even tragedies, that, throughout, have been entwined with the work. 6**

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a list of [aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation "Aviation")-related events from 1908:

*   The [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") announces plans to buy flying machines.
*   [Fiat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat "Fiat") begins to manufacture aero engines.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-1)
*   The French aircraft designer and manufacturer [Édouard Nieuport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Nieuport "Édouard Nieuport") begins the construction of [his first aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nieuport_1909_monoplane&action=edit&redlink=1 "Nieuport 1909 monoplane (page does not exist)"), a small [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") powered by a 20-[horsepower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsepower "Horsepower") (15-[kilowatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilowatt "Kilowatt")) [Darracq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobiles_Darracq_France "Automobiles Darracq France") engine.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-2)

*   8 January – Count [Ferdinand von Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_von_Zeppelin "Ferdinand von Zeppelin") announces plans to build an [airship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship") capable of carrying 100 passengers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Daniel,_Clifton_1987,_p._108-3)
*   13 January – [Henri Farman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Farman "Henri Farman") wins the [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")10,000 [Deutsch-Archdeacon Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Archdeacon#Sponsor_of_aviation "Ernest Archdeacon") for making the world's first circular flight of at least 1 km (0.62 mi) in a [Voisin 1907 biplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voisin_1907_biplane "Voisin 1907 biplane"). In a flight of 1 minute 28 seconds at [Issy-les-Moulineaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issy-les-Moulineaux "Issy-les-Moulineaux"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), he flies well over a kilometer at an altitude of 25 to 30 feet (7.6 to 9.1 meters).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Daniel,_Clifton_1987,_p._108-3)
*   March – [Michelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin "Michelin") announces the [Michelin Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin_Cup "Michelin Cup"), a prize to be awarded for the longest distance covered by an airplane in a single flight during the calendar year, beginning with 1908. Initially, the prize is be presented annually for a period of eight years.
*   17 March – [AEA Red Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA_Red_Wing "AEA Red Wing") is destroyed in a crash on its second flight.
*   21 March – [Henri Farman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Farman "Henri Farman") makes the first flight carrying a passenger in a [biplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biplane "Biplane").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-4)

*   14 May – [Charles Furnas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Furnas "Charles Furnas") becomes the first passenger in an aeroplane in the United States, piloted by [Wilbur Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Brothers "Wright Brothers"). They fly for a distance of approximately 600m in 28-3/5ths seconds in the [Wright 1905 Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Flyer_III "Wright Flyer III"), modified with seats for pilot and passenger. Shortly after, [Orville Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Brothers "Wright Brothers") flies Furnas for 4.12 km in 4 minutes 2-2/5ths seconds.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCKH-5)
*   22 May – The [Wright brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_brothers "Wright brothers") register their airplane with the [United States Patent Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_Office "United States Patent Office").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-6)
*   31 May – Henry Farman is reported[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Peltier-7) to have flown with a Mlle. P. Van Pottelsberghe de la Potterie, daughter of the mayor of Desteldonk in [Ghent, Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghent,_Belgium "Ghent, Belgium"). She is the first woman passenger in an aeroplane.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-8)
*   June – [Alliott Verdon Roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliott_Verdon_Roe "Alliott Verdon Roe") performs taxiing and towed flight trials with his first powered aeroplane at [Brooklands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklands "Brooklands"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey").
*   28 June – [Jacob Ellehammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Ellehammer "Jacob Ellehammer") makes the first piloted, powered aeroplane flight in Germany.

*   The [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy")'s Director of Naval Ordnance, [Captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(naval) "Captain (naval)")[Reginald Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reginald_Bacon "Reginald Bacon"), recommends that the Royal Navy acquire an [airship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship") to compete with the [_Kaiserliche Marine_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_German_Navy "Imperial German Navy")'s [Zeppelins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeppelin "Zeppelin").
*   4 July – [Glenn H. Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_H._Curtiss "Glenn H. Curtiss") is awarded the _[Scientific American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific\_American "Scientific American")_ trophy for being the first person in the United States to make a public flight of over 1 km (0.62 mi) in the [AEA June Bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA_June_Bug "AEA June Bug").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-9) The award is for a flight at [Hammondsport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammondsport "Hammondsport") in which he flies 1,550 m (5,090 ft) in 1 minute and 42 seconds.
*   8 July – [Thérèse Peltier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9r%C3%A8se_Peltier "Thérèse Peltier") officially becomes the first woman to fly in an aeroplane. She is a passenger on a flight made by [Léon Delagrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Delagrange "Léon Delagrange") at [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"). However, this flight may not have been fully controlled.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Delagrange-10) See also [#May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#May) and [#October](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#October).
*   30 July – Seeking a venue to host aviation events in the [Grand Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Paris "Grand Paris") (Greater Paris) region of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") better than the [racetracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racetrack "Racetrack") and military maneuver grounds used previously, the _Société d’Encouragement à l’Aviation_ (Society for the Encouragement of Aviation) is formed to establish the world's first true airfield designed specifically for the use of aviators, as well as the world's first aviation school and first aviation competition. The Society's work will result in the opening of [Port-Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-Aviation "Port-Aviation"), an aviation event venue considered the world's first purpose-built airfield, in [1909](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1909_in_aviation "1909 in aviation").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-13)
*   8 August – Wilbur Wright makes his first flights at the [Hunaudières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunaudi%C3%A8res "Hunaudières") racetrack at [Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans "Le Mans"), France. The Wright Flyer used for this and later flights had been shipped to [Le Havre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Havre "Le Havre") by Orville the previous year. It had been seriously damaged by custom officials when it arrived in France and was uncrated. Wilbur spent the whole summer of 1908 rebuilding the machine and getting it into flying condition. Wilbur's flights in this machine will have a profound effect on European aviation during the following months.
*   9 August – In the [Ferber IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferber_IX "Ferber IX"), French aviator [Georges Legagneux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Legagneux "Georges Legagneux") makes a flight at [Issy-les-Moulineaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issy-les-Moulineaux "Issy-les-Moulineaux"), France, that wins him the [Aero Club de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_Club_de_France "Aero Club de France")'s third and final 200-metre (656 ft) prize.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-14) He will be retrospectively disqualified in September for making the flight too early in the morning.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-15)
*   20 August – [Robert Gastambide](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Gastambide&action=edit&redlink=1 "Robert Gastambide (page does not exist)") becomes the first passenger carried by a [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") when he is taken up on the [Antoinette II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoinette_II "Antoinette II").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Donald,_David_1997,_p._52-16)
*   21 August 
    *   Wilbur Wright moves to Camp d'Auvours, 11 kilometres (6.8 mi) east of Le Mans, where all his flights for the remainder of the year will be based.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCCD-17)
    *   The [Antoinette II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoinette_II "Antoinette II") flies the first circle by a monoplane.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Donald,_David_1997,_p._52-16)

*   3 September – Seeking a contract to build the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army")'s first airplane, Orville Wright begins flight trials before Army observers at [Fort Myer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Myer "Fort Myer"), [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), in a new [Wright Model A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Model_A "Wright Model A") flyer. The flight lasts 1 minute 11 seconds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Boys_1989,_p._374-18)
*   6 September – [Léon Delagrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Delagrange "Léon Delagrange") sets distance and endurance records with a flight of 24.727 kilometres (15.365 mi) lasting 29 minutes 53.8 seconds at [Issy-les-Moulineaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issy-les-Moulineaux "Issy-les-Moulineaux"), France.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-19)
*   9 September – At Fort Myer, Orville Wright sets three world records: a flight endurance record of 57 minutes 13 seconds on his first flight, a new flight endurance record of 1 hour 2 minutes and 15 seconds on his second flight (the world's first airplane flight of over one hour), and an endurance record for a flight with a passenger (Army [Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant "Lieutenant")[Frank P. Lahm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Purdy_Lahm "Frank Purdy Lahm")) of 6 minutes 24 seconds on his third flight.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Boys_1989,_p._374-18)
*   10 September – At Fort Myer, Orville Wright sets a world flight endurance record of 1 hour 5 minutes and 52 seconds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Boys_1989,_p._374-18)
*   11 September – At Fort Myer, Orville Wright sets a world flight endurance record of 1 hour 10 minutes and 24 seconds.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-20)
*   12 September – At Fort Myer, Orville Wright sets a world record for flight endurance with a passenger (Army [Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_(rank) "Major (rank)")[George O. Squier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Owen_Squier "George Owen Squier")) of 9 minutes 6+1⁄3 seconds.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-21)
*   17 September – U.S. Army [Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant "Lieutenant")[Thomas Selfridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Selfridge "Thomas Selfridge") becomes the first person killed in a powered aircraft crash and the first military aviation casualty when the [Wright Model A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Model_A "Wright Model A"), piloted by Orville Wright during U.S. Army tests, suffers a broken propeller and crashes from an altitude of 75 feet (23 meters) at Fort Myer. Wright is severely injured.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCKH-5)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-22)
*   [Thérèse Peltier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9r%C3%A8se_Peltier "Thérèse Peltier") makes a flight of 200 metres (656 feet) at a height of approximately 2.5 meters (8.2 feet) at the Military Square in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). Photos of Peltier with the aeroplane are published on 27 September.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Peltier-7) Unofficially, it is the first flight by a female aviator.
*   28 September – At Camp d'Avours, France, [Wilbur Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Wright "Wilbur Wright") sets a world airplane endurance record in a flight of 1 hour 32 minutes, covering 61 miles (98 km), winning a [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")1,000 prize from the [Aero Club of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_Club_of_France "Aero Club of France") for the longest flight in history over an enclosed ground.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Daniel,_Clifton_1987,_p._117-23)

*   3 October – George P. Dicken of the _[New York Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Herald "New York Herald")_ becomes the first [newspaper reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper_reporter "Newspaper reporter") to fly in an airplane when he rides as a passenger with [Wilbur Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Wright "Wilbur Wright") at Camp d'Auvours.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-24) The flight sets a world record for the longest with a passenger, lasting 55 minutes 37 seconds.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Daniel,_Clifton_1987,_p._117-23)
*   5 October – The [Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeppelin "Zeppelin")_LZ IV_ is destroyed by fire at [Echterdingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echterdingen_Airport "Echterdingen Airport"), Germany.
*   6 October – At Camp d'Avours, Wilbur Wright sets another world record for a flight with a passenger, remaining aloft for 1 hour 4 minutes 26 seconds. He wins a $100,000 prize from a French syndicate for making two record-setting flights with a passenger within the same week.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Daniel,_Clifton_1987,_p._117-23)
*   7 October – Wilbur Wright flies with [Edith Ogilby Berg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Ogilby_Berg "Edith Ogilby Berg"), aka Mrs. [Hart O. Berg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart_O._Berg "Hart O. Berg"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Berg-25) as passenger at Camp d'Auvours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCCD-17) This is the first fully controlled flight with a woman passenger.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Delagrange-10)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Berg-25)
*   16 October – [Samuel Cody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Cody "Samuel Cody") makes his first aeroplane flight in the United Kingdom in [British Army Aeroplane No. 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army_Aeroplane_No._1 "British Army Aeroplane No. 1").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-26)
*   18 October – Wilbur Wright climbs to 115 metres (377 ft) above Camp d'Auvours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCCD-17)
*   30 October – Henry Farman makes the first cross-country flight in a power-driven aeroplane, flying from [Bouy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouy "Bouy") to [Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reims "Reims") 27 kilometres (17 mi) in 20 minutes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-27)
*   November – Horace, Eustace, and [Oswald Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_Short "Oswald Short") found [Short Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_Brothers "Short Brothers"), the first aircraft manufacturing company in England, in [Battersea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea "Battersea"), London.
*   1 November – Flights begin from the world's first purpose-built airfield, [Port-Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-Aviation "Port-Aviation") (often called "Juvisy Airfield") in [Viry-Chatillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viry-Chatillon "Viry-Chatillon") in the [Grand Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Paris "Grand Paris") (Greater Paris) region of France, when the _Ligue National Aérienne_ (National Aviation League) opens a flying school there operating two [Voisin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voisin "Voisin") airplanes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-firstpurposebuilt-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-premiera%C3%A9rodromep20-29) The school's instructor is [Ferdinand Ferber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Ferber "Ferdinand Ferber"), and [Igor Sikorsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Sikorsky "Igor Sikorsky") enrolls for flying lessons.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-premiera%C3%A9rodromep20-29) Port-Aviation remains under construction and will not open officially until [1909](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1909_in_aviation "1909 in aviation").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-30)
*   3 November – An [Aeronautical Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York") exhibition takes place at [Morris Park Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome "Morris Park Aerodrome").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-31)
*   18 December 
    *   Wilbur Wright at [Camp d'Auvours](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Camp_d%27Auvours&action=edit&redlink=1 "Camp d'Auvours (page does not exist)")([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auvours "fr:Auvours")), 11 kilometres (6.8 miles) east of [Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans "Le Mans"), France, flies 99.8 kilometres (62.0 mi) in 1 hour 54 minutes 2/5 second, rising to an altitude of 110 meters (361 feet) – a new world record.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCCD-17)
    *   American [aeronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronaut "Aeronaut") and [aerial photographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_photographer "Aerial photographer")[Melvin Vaniman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Vaniman "Melvin Vaniman") flies a steel-tube-frame [triplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triplane "Triplane") he designed and built himself a distance of 150 meters (490 feet) above the [parade ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade_ground "Parade ground") at [Issy-les-Moulineaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issy-les-Moulineaux "Issy-les-Moulineaux"), France.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-32)

*   24 December – The first Paris Aeronautical Salon opens the Grand Palais.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-33)
*   31 December – Wilbur Wright sets a new nonstop distance record for an airplane, flying 123.2 kilometres (76.6 mi) on a triangular course in 2 hours 18 minutes 33.2 seconds at Camp d'Auvours in [Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans "Le Mans"), France. He wins the 1908 [Michelin Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin_Cup "Michelin Cup"), a prize of [FF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_franc "French franc")20,000 from [Michelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin "Michelin"), for the longest nonstop distance in a single flight in 1908.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-USCoFCCD-17)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-34)

*   12 March - [AEA Red Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA_Red_Wing "AEA Red Wing"), flying from the surface of [Keuka Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keuka_Lake "Keuka Lake") near [Hammondsport, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammondsport,_New_York "Hammondsport, New York"). Flight distance is 97.2 metres (319 ft) but ends with the aircraft collapsing to the ground, leaving the pilot slightly bruised. This is the first public demonstration of a powered aircraft flight in the United States.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-Washington_Post-35)
*   18 May - [AEA White Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA_White_Wing "AEA White Wing")
*   8 June - [Roe I Biplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_I_Biplane "Roe I Biplane")
*   21 June - [AEA June Bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA_June_Bug "AEA June Bug")
*   By 30 June - [Blériot VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bl%C3%A9riot_VIII "Blériot VIII"), undated flight of some 730 metres (2,395 ft) at [Issy-les-Moulineaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issy-les-Moulineaux "Issy-les-Moulineaux"), France[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_in_aviation#cite_note-36)

*   5 September - [Goupy No.1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goupy_No.1 "Goupy No.1"), the world's first triplane
*   19 October - [Antoinette IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoinette_IV "Antoinette IV")
*   6 December - [AEA Silver Dart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA_Silver_Dart "AEA Silver Dart")

Retrieved November 23, 2018. In the new year, 1908, Blériot built another, No.VII, which similarly crashed, and then another, No. VIII, which met the same fate. These planes were covered with rice paper to keep weight to a minimum. Blériot's tenacity and enthusiasm sprang from his "passion for the problems of aviation" - his own words for his devotion to flying. And his persistence was paying off. His new machines were generally better than their predecessors and in No. VIII he flew for 800 yards (730 m).) at Issy. This machine had a 50 h.p. Antoinette, and good controls, including large 'modern' ailerons on the trailing edge of the wing. On 6 July he stayed aloft for 8.5 minutes: his best time yet.

13.title: America's Aeronautical Pioneers
13.content:
By Lieutenant Horace S. Mazet, U. S. Marine Corps Reserve

Flying burst upon a startled and incredulous world in 1903, with the Wright Brothers the _dei ex machina_. Yet, by 1906, there were still only two men who could fly.

Almost at once thereafter, however, owing to many contributing causes, not the least of which was an expansion program conducted by the co-inventors of man-flight, a pronounced aviation urge swept over the country which had given it birth. By January 1, 1911, there were at least 1,000 daring men who could fly heavier-than-air machines. Western Europe led all the rest of the world in the promotion and acceptance of this new mode of travel and entertainment.

In America much of what progress there was in the air was traceable to the efforts of an optimistic group who called themselves the Aeronautical Society of America. It is to this body of enthusiasts that the honor goes of being the first actual purchaser of a flying machine. Yet, strangely enough, their program which was admittedly vague and their zealous espousal of a cause yet to be proved, as against years of successful lighter-than-air experiments, evoked general scorn, ridicule, and actual opposition from newspapers and pseudo-altruistic aeronautical groups. Bad luck, also, lost no time in visiting the organization as well as the individual plane builders thereof, while a sneering lack of faith on the part of the public persisted.

But the Aeronautical Society was founded on stern stuff, and saw visions with a practical eye. In all, fifty men in various professions, mechanics, scientists, business men, and wealthy men, answered the call to boom the new society; they believed in aviation and moved with the determination of faith to partake of the achievement spirit abroad in the land.

That American aviation was to benefit from this as yet blind belief in the efficacy of heavier-than-air craft was the fond hope of the organizers. That it did in reality is a distinct tribute to the persistence, unanimity, devotion, and earnest effort which characterized the young society from the start, particularly in the face of denunciatory criticism. The charter declared the intention of the new body to be the fostering and aiding in the development and encouragement of the new art of flying by all means within its power. It was not limited to advice and monetary subsidy alone; members of the unit were fully determined to plunge into the game themselves and emerge either with broken bones and hopes or with airplanes that would actually fly. In particular, members who had recently been affiliated with the Aero Club and its reactionary beliefs in the supremacy of ballooning, were out to show that it was eminently practical to lift one’s self by one’s bootstraps even if, to date, birdmen were themselves a little uncertain about flying machines and their idiosyncracies.

A committee was appointed to secure grounds and sheds for active experimentation. Then a greater step was proposed and carried: to advance aviation in the country, the society invited the famed French airman, Delagrange, to visit America for a flying exhibition that would stimulate the entire nation with the possibilities of flight.

Flying was news; they meant to capitalize on it willy-nilly. If they could not immediately fly, they would get someone who could. And since Delagrange had just made a world’s record duration flight of fifteen minutes, he was sure to “make” every front page in the country.

No sooner was the news out than the opposition countered with an urgent invitation to another famous flier, Henri Farman, whose importation from France was relied upon to produce much revenue and profit for the syndicate of St. Louis schemers and the antagonistic Aero Club. Exhibition fliers at that time were paid no mere pittance, $10,000 for one flight was not unheard of, and as a rule individual airmen would clean up during a year of successful flights, although none of them might have been for more than ten-minutes duration or of greater height than a dozen feet or so.

The society conferred. Feeling that open warfare would benefit American aviation little, the directors moved to withdraw their plan for Delagrange in favor of Farman and his coterie of St. Louis backers with their rosy-tinted publicity. No resentful body was this! When Farman arrived, he was greeted by representatives of the Aeronautical Society which had indeed taken him to their collective heart. Farman was feted at dinners and receptions, while his machine was made ready at a race track at Brighton Beach, Long Island.

Shortly, however, trouble loomed on the horizon. The exhibitions were not paying in cash. People found that the touted flight was more likely a hop—and it might just as well be witnessed from a near-by promontory without payment. Moreover, weather, or rather playful breezes, proved extremely formidable. A slight wind was enough to warrant cancellation of any projected trip aloft. And so Farman, before long, was found in the predicament of having to pay numerous bills which according to agreement, were to have been defrayed by his backers. Time passed and brought no settlement. Farman was threatened with arrest. The remainder of the exhibitions were called off.

But once again the society was ready. On a certain evening, William J. Hammer and Anthony Triaca, fellow-directors of the heavier-than-air exponents, took charge of Farman, packed up his plane and arranged for his safe conduct to a steamer soon sailing for France. Deputy sheriffs with attachments hove in sight, two hours later, but their birdman had flown.

Who could blame Farman for feeling embittered? Yet he later somewhat forgave America, his good nature coming to the rescue, and became an honorary member of the Aeronautical Society.

The first of the week-end gatherings which were to become well known took place at Morris Park in upper Manhattan. A lease had been obtained here until 1911, and it was proposed to use this place for flights and building airplanes. Great as were the soaring hopes on that first Saturday afternoon when members of the pioneering society met to look over the property, none imagined the strides which were to be made within an exceedingly short time. And here again the society contributed to the history of aeronautics, for this occasion marked the first time that any group of citizens had ever leased a bit of land for the purposes of mechanical flight. This was the beginning of the great airports of the world.

There was definite incentive for construction and attempts at flight. A silver cup was offered for the member whose personally built machine was the first in the air. Thus spurred on by the honor of being the first successful builder, the hitherto visionary members were now caught in the throes of a furious spurt of activity. None, dreaming of that gleaming silver cup, imagined the tremendous rise and fall of hopes which were to take place before any member's craft rose in a great struggle from the dark womb of earth and set forth upon wings of its own. On the other hand, none could foresee that within a few months the society was to take the most important step in its career, which would win for America the biggest international trophy in world aviation.

Paying as little attention as possible to caustic criticism from the press and the public generally, the society did not waver. Wilbur R. Kimball, a young genius with leanings toward vertical flight, finally finished the society's first machine. It was an awe-inspiring spectacle. On a frame work of bicycle tubing there was a seat and a small engine. Overhead were twenty-four 2-foot propellers which whirred menacingly on a wide framework. The creation snorted and shook. But this great contribution to the art of flight did not win the silver cup because it could not meet the one condition required: it would not fly.

At the same time almost every other member was hard at work on a machine of his own, or helping another with his idea of what a real sky-traveling vehicle should be. Membership mounted, and soon there was not a vacant hangar to be found. Then, _mirabile dictu_, in 1909 a large number of the members of the distinctly uppish Aero Club of America resigned in high dudgeon at the ruling faction’s anachronistic belief in the divinity of lighter-than-air craft, and joined the Aeronautical Society!

Morris Park, the open-air laboratory, could claim no hill worthy of the name, and some means of imparting initial impetus was sought. The Wright catapult being considered a bit dangerous, a tower was constructed, from the top of which any glider might launch his craft upon the wings of the wind in any direction. As it happened, one enthusiast declined to be disheartened by a lack of breeze. He therefore stayed atop the wooden structure built by Dr. S. B. Battey nearly the whole of one day waiting for favor from the heavens. A building permit for the erection of this tower having been (pardonably) overlooked, the city building department of New York took official cognizance of the lapse, decided that the length of occupancy had converted the structure into a dwelling, and so, as it had neither plumbing nor fire escape, condemned it as unfit for residential purposes and solemnly ordered its removal. It was demolished, and thereafter gliders were towed into the wind by a weight-catapult device as originated by the Wright Brothers.

Increasing interest in aviation, toward which the newspapers were being won over, influenced the society to hold a series of exhibitions of models and plans. Results exceeded the most sanguine expectations.

When cold weather set in, winter quarters for the 200-odd members were opened by invitation in the Automobile Club of America. On February 9, 1909, the first full-dress aeronautical evening took place with enthusiasm running high. Upon this gala occasion Hudson Maxim, later president of the society, gave an address on his views of the future of flying machines in war. Col. Butler Ames, M.C., lectured, and Mr. M. O. Anthony demonstrated his experimental wireless control of airships. Such talks, interesting in themselves, and significant of the diversified tastes of the group’s interests, initiated the lecture series which was to run during the greater part of the society’s history and contributed in no small way to aeronautical progress in America.

With the year 1909, the members felt that it should do something definite to encourage the art on a much wider scale. They turned to a young and promising builder who was making actual flights in planes of his own construction, and doing it very well indeed. Glenn Curtiss was chosen as a fit subject to receive the collective encouragement of the group, and a contract was drawn up, but kept secret between them until Curtiss should officially sever his connection with Dr. Alexander Graham Bell’s Aerial Experiment Association, an organization delving into the physical laws of flight and making abortive efforts to get off the earth.

For the sum of $5,000, Curtiss agreed to build an airplane for the society. The contract thus drawn marked the first purchase of an airplane anywhere, and was the beginning of commercial aviation in the world. The First Aero Syndicate, which purchased this machine, was composed of the following members of the society: Lee S. Burridge, William J. Hammer, Orrel Parker, Louis R. Adams, C. W. Howell, Julian P. Thomas, Herbert C. Smythe, Frank C. Burridge, E. T. Tandy, R. E. Sabin, C. W. Howell, Jr., Frank G. Smith, Jr., E. W. Cameron, C. F. Block- more, Jas. M. Fisher, Carlos de Zafra, Jas. P. Hill, E. T. Birdsall, F. A. Scheffler, O. A. Danielson, J. P. Stalz, Ernest L. Jones, Michael A. Whalen, George Bold, Albert Huth, Wm. A. Kelley, and Dr. S. B. Battey.

Written into the contract was a clause providing for the instruction of two society members by Mr. Curtiss personally in the art of flying. In July, 1909, Charles Wilard, taking his indoctrination on the front porch of the flimsy crates of that bygone day, made his first flight of 500 feet touched the ground, bounced for another 200 feet, and landed safely. Curtiss congratulated him, saying it was a better flight than his own first attempt. An early bird had been born.

The second member to try his luck was Alex Williams, and in his eagerness, he ascended too rapidly, gained 50 feet, and crashed to the ground, fracturing the machine and his arm and thumb, but the damage was repaired without complications and others were soon clamoring for a flight. The society machine in the air was a tremendous impetus to the member builders who still had their eye on that silver cup.

Increased activity was in evidence at the various sheds and hangars of the Morris Park field. A huge triplane was completed by Morris Bokor, and it under went many changes in design before it finally seemed to suit the aberrant aero dynamical convictions of its builder, but it eventually won a prize of $500 for excellence in design and construction at a competition in Arlington, N. J., thus evidently vindicating his judgment. Strange as it may seem, however, the machine never got over its obstinate refusal to leave Mother Earth.

But now the time was coming when the eyes of the flying world would be centered on the International Gordon Bennett race at Rheims, France. The title of world champion automatically festooned the wind-lashed brow of the first across the finish line in this contest, and renowned aviators of all countries planned to flock to the meet on the appointed day. America wanted representation, but the Wright Brothers, premier native birdmen, had disposed of their spectacular airplane to the War Department the fall previous and were occupied with construction work. Mr. Curtiss then approached the society.

Would the society be willing to let him copy their machine for an entry in the international meet? They would. Consequently work started on a replica of the Curtiss-made contraption, while the original was transported to Hempstead Plains, Long Island, where Curtiss practiced flying for the coming contest. Aeronautical and patriotic feeling ran high. Work was pushed on the racing plane, but it did not attain completion in time for it to be flight tested. Nevertheless, go it must, and it as boxed up and sent abroad without having been in the air. Mr. Curtiss followed with the heartfelt enthusiasm of the society and all air-minded America.

Curtiss won! The society's collective hat went sailing into the air also, and now for the first time it felt that unqualified approval was forthcoming from the press and the public at large. It had indeed placed America upon the aeronautical map with a vengeance, and Glenn Curtiss' name became a by-word among news-reading peoples.

Then, in September, the silver cup was finally won. It went to the builders of the Raiche-Crout biplane. Other members' flying machines which actually flew (some of them well) were rapidly completed. Among these were ships built by Pincus Brauner and A. J. Smith, Dr. William Green, whose 2-passenger pusher was the first to employ an ordinary stock model automobile engine in flight, Riggs and Rice (a dirigible), and Frank van Anden. Dr. Henry Walden the flying dentist of Brooklyn, built not one machine but thirteen, the last eleven of which flew. His successful craft were all monoplanes, the first in America. Dozens of other members were fiddling with propellers, engines, gliders, balloons, and parachutes with interesting if not always practical results. There were even wind machines propelled by man power, and glider contests staged at various flying fields in which the society had an interest.

With the advent of the Hudson-Fulton celebration, the society reached a new high in providing amazing spectacles. It was generally agreed that the new art of flying should be brought to the attention of the public, so the society, through its energetic and ubiquitous member William J. Hammer, made all the necessary arrangements and got Wilbur Wright to make a reluctant flight around the Statue of Liberty. This served to focus the attention of the nation on flying, but when, a day or so later, he completed his epoch-making excursion of twenty-one miles, up the Hudson to Grant’s Tomb and around the international war fleet anchored in the river and back to Governors Island, landing within a few feet of his starting point, he stirred the world and thrilled the watchers as nothing else could have done.

A most signal achievement in the society’s history was the banquet at the Hotel Astor on April 27, 1911, at which the President of the United States was the honored guest. Approximately 900 other guests were present, besides the Honorable William Howard Taft. On the speaker’s table was placed a collection of scale model airplanes, and when the time came to clear away after the festivities, Hammer, in charge as usual, could not find his models. The society threatened to turn the hotel upside down unless they were produced, and finally a search discovered them hidden in the tiny room of a German waiter. That is, all except the model of the original Wright plane, which had been made by the Wrights themselves. It had been placed directly in front of Admiral Peary, but everyone denied having seen it after the dinner, and it has never turned up.

Activity afield and in the air was rife thereafter, for aviation had infected many people with its strange virus. Now that America was addicted to watching flying exhibitions, which rapidly became more prevalent, there was a new and more somber note apparent in aviation. It was one of morbidity. Crowds flocked to meets and competitive flights to be sure not to miss a good smash-up. The more spectacular fliers earned for themselves the nickname of dare-devils, and not without reason; they earned for themselves also tremendous salaries when not under contract to exhibition companies. And they sooner or later dove their planes once too often, or tried flying under bridges that were too low.

In fact, by 1912, the situation in the flying world was peculiar. Practically all of the earlier fliers with the exception of a notable few were killed off in the exercise of their profession. As a consequence the public held the general impression that the airplane was hardly better than a device for the perpetration of hair-raising stunts.

It was up to clear-thinking agencies to combat this detrimental impression. Such stigma was exactly what the Aeronautical Society at this time actively had to combat if its years of effort and contribution were to be of lasting value. In this pursuit it therefore engaged as doggedly as it had, four years before, in espousing the cause of aviation itself; papers, lectures, and appearances before other engineering societies geared to the sane promotion of the art were the means. And flying exhibitions, so dear to the heart of every member, were discontinued largely because the society felt that the time was ripe for solid engineering advance rather than for spectacular performances for the public.

Gradually—owing as much to the cessation of flights by members as any one factor—the society began to shift from an experimental and flying body to an engineering, discoursive, consultation organization of practical men. Its mental horizon extended far beyond the flying field, which was comparatively deserted, and the interests of individual members, to encompass the country as a whole and its aeronautical and aerodynamic problems. The society machine had long since been sold.

Members were no longer anxious to spend their money on new airplanes which might not fly well. The consensus of the society’s personnel at the crossroads was, generally speaking, logically in favor of the shift, led as it was by such leaders as Hudson Maxim, illustrious brother of the machine-gun inventor, R. R. Grant, chief production engineer later at McCook Field, Elmer A. Sperry of gyroscopic fame, William g, J. Hammer later of the General Staff, U.S.A., and Gutzon Borglum, and it lent its attention to more basic aviation problems of the nation.

On March 5, 1914, the society in a letter to the Commissioner of Navigation, Department of Commerce, urged the governmental licensing of aircraft operators and the registration of aircraft. Fourteen years later, the government complied.

The entry of the United States into the war threw the organization of the Aeronautical Society into a frenzy of service. Mathew Sellers, Hudson Maxim, and Howard E. Coffin were elected by invitation of Secretary of the Navy Daniels to the Naval Consulting Board in 1917. Because of this the nose of the Aero Club, which had not been invited to participate was considerably out of joint. But its previous constructive history was such that by comparison the Aeronautical Society far outshone its waning rival, and the remonstrance was the last gasp of the Aero Club, essentially a sporting and balloon club.

William J. Hammer was chosen unanimously to go to Washington and become the first outside member of the Naval Consulting Board in 1917, but he withdrew in favor of Maxim and Sellers, with had many friends and were quite familiar with technical details, both being students of aerodynamics. Later, Hammer was pleased that he took this step, for he was called to Washington, and, despite lack of any military experience, was made a member of the General Staff of the U. S. Army with rank of Major, being put in charge of the inventions and patents section of the War Plans Division (I think I am correct), and made frequent flights over Washington with military pilots to test the efficiency of various devices offered to the government. He served with distinction throughout the war. Hammer has also been awarded the cross of the Legion of Honor from France for work he did there with the original French Edison Company in the eighties as head of the European Edison organization.

Other members of the society were Lieutenant Frederick W. Humphreys, U. S. Army (one of first Wright fliers); Captain W. I. Chambers, U. S. Navy; Ralph H. Upson, famous balloonist in international competitions; Lee De Forest, later a famous radio engineer and inventor; Grover C. Loening, builder of the Navy Loening amphibians. Octave Chanute, noted glider, and Wm. Randolph Hearst were honorary members, as were E. I. du Pont, Isaac Guggenheim, F. A. Sieberling, and Inglis M. Uppercu.

Real work for the society—despite immediate and hearty co-operation with Howard E. Coffin under the auspices of the Naval Consulting Board in investigating manufacturing facilities of the United States in preparation for over-seas aerial combat—did not start, however, until General Tasker Bliss asked that a committee of the society come to Washington to confer on designing an airplane with folding wings that could run on the highways like an automobile, then spread out its wings and fly. An abortive creation was constructed, contrary to the counsel of the society, but there the matter has lain to this day. The craft never flew.

The problem of the Aeronautical Society to encourage every form of inventive aeronautics and yet to co-operate with the government was considerably complicated in September, 1917, when aircraft manufacturers pooled all patents. The society vigorously protested against this arrangement as being apt to delay the development of aircraft and stifle invention in the field. Yet in the exigency of war time there were none to heed the cries of those whose toes were trampled, and the society had to swallow its pride along with the opinion of the attorney general on this matter, asked for by Secretary of War Newton D. Baker as a result of the protest.

Activities of the society reached a peak about the beginning of 1918. The aeronautical program, for the execution of which Congress had appropriated $640,000,000, by this time had practically collapsed. Liberty engines were not forthcoming; casualties in training camps were excessive; factories produced few training planes. Still, optimistic reports were constantly issuing from the publicity, departments of the government.

The society met, and urged that something be done. It was decided at that unlucky meeting to co-operate with Mr. Gutzon Borglum, society member, famous sculptor, and friend of President Wilson.

Borglum wrote to Wilson, telling him of the society’s grave doubts as to whether all that could be done was in fact being done in aircraft production.

The President replied in a short letter, instructing Borglum to investigate the situation. The sculptor, no coward, took him at his word, used the letter freely as an “open sesame,” and began his campaign. Being an artist and not a politician he gave out the results of his investigation in the form of an interview with the press.

The papers published the interview in anything but temperate language, and it produced an impression similar to that of an aerial bomb dropped on a gasoline dump. The main facts—or at least some of them—in the Borglum indictment were unquestionably correct. Others, however, were merely garbled or gossip. Thus the danger was that disproval of parts of the criticism might lead to a general conviction that all was serene in the government aircraft departments.

Under such tense conditions the report of the Aeronautical Society, based upon the Borglum findings, was published in April, 1918. It was introduced to the public in a rather spectacular meeting in New York, where one of the speakers was Representative John Q. Tilson of Connecticut. The entire report was republished as a United States document and it led to the appointment of Mr. Charles Evans Hughes, now Chief Justice, as an investigator of the aircraft situation. But no definite action was taken, other more pressing matters cropping up before long.

The result of the publication of their aircraft report on the fate of the Aeronautical Society was disastrous. Official Washington’s attitude was such that many members connected with the war-time government had to resign. All official courtesies were removed, and the society was no longer invited to participate in the development of engineering problems for the aircraft administration and the fighting branches. The usefulness of the society had indeed passed, and even the meetings were no longer held.

The Aeronautical Society in its heyday performed a very essential service by popularizing the possibilities of heavier-than-air craft and by materially encouraging American inventors in the perfection of their devices. Regardless of war-time disfavor, the society also performed a patriotic service in many administrative branches, not the least of which was that very act of calling to public attention certain defects in the government's program of aircraft construction. For these were ultimately remedied.

And finally, the wind-up, decline, and disintegration of the society after the Armistice was largely natural in view of the general tendency in those days to shun all that reminded the country of war. It was the dawn of the Aviation Age.
